Geography: eight-section lesson guide

Select a lesson. These are the same explanations and checks available on each slide in the classroom player.

The route is planned for 40 minutes: recall, goal, vocabulary, explanation, worked example, student practice, check and exit ticket. Students practise in exercise books or on the board after seeing a model.

Timings are planning estimates. Classroom teaching duration has not been measured; the guide contains substantive explanations rather than instructions to prolong a short activity.

Landscape detectives

7A · Week 2 · sections 1.1

40-minute route: recall 4, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 8, worked example 5, practice 10, check 5, exit 3. Divide each section between the topics in combined lessons. Timings are estimates.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

How can one school place involve both people and nature?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. A garden has plants and soil, while people plant and water it. Connect this to today’s task: Landscape detectives.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can classify a feature and explain an interaction.

On screen: Today’s task: Landscape detectives / You will make labelled features and a connection diagram. / Name the physical and human features. / Explain an action linking people and nature. / Separate observations from predictions.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: labelled features and a connection diagram. Explain the three criteria: Name the physical and human features. Explain an action linking people and nature. Separate observations from predictions. The independent task uses this case: Our model valley contains a river, wooded slope, houses, bridge and cleared land.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Physical geography: Natural features and processes. Soil and plants in a school garden. / Human geography: People, places and activities. People build and use the path. / Interaction: How people and nature affect each other. A pupil waters the plants.

Physical geography: Natural features and processes. Example: Soil and plants in a school garden. Human geography: People, places and activities. Example: People build and use the path. Interaction: How people and nature affect each other. Example: A pupil waters the plants. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Geography asks about places

On screen: What is here? Where is it? / Why is it here? How does it affect people?

Geography helps us understand places and the connections between them. Start with our classroom. The building has a location, people use it, and its surroundings influence how we reach it. Now move out to the school, the town and the world. These are different scales of study. A question about one street needs local detail; a question about countries needs a wider view. Geography joins information about nature and people rather than treating a place as a list of names.

Brief check: Which question asks about location?
Listen for: “Where is it?” asks about location.

Physical and human features

On screen: Physical: river, hill, soil. / Human: road, bridge, building.

Physical geography studies natural features and processes. Human geography studies people and their activities. Point to the river and describe its water and banks. Then point to the bridge and describe what people built. A feature can involve both. A farm uses soil, plants and rainfall, but people choose crops and manage the land. Do not tell pupils that every feature must fit only one box. The categories help us explain a place; they do not remove the connections between its parts.

Brief check: Why can a farm involve both categories?
Listen for: Natural soil and rainfall support human farming activities.

People and nature affect each other

On screen: Rain can affect a road. / A road can affect rainwater flow.

An interaction is a connection in which things affect each other. Heavy rain can make a road difficult to use. Building a road can also change the ground: a paved surface may allow less water into soil, so more water may move over the surface. Trace each direction with an arrow. The first starts with a natural process and ends with a human activity. The second starts with construction and ends with water movement. We need evidence to find the size of an effect in a real place.

Brief check: Can the connection work in both directions?
Listen for: Yes. Nature affects people, and people change their environment.

What does “make a link” mean?

On screen: A link explains how two things affect each other. / The bridge crosses the river, so people can reach the other bank.

Compare two sentences. “River, bridge, school” lists three features. “The bridge crosses the river, so pupils can reach the school from the other bank” explains a connection. Point to each feature while saying its part of the sentence. The word so joins an action to an effect. Because introduces a reason. A useful geographical explanation tells us how the connection works. “The bridge is good” gives a judgement without explaining it. Ask the class which words show what the bridge actually does.

Brief check: What is missing from a list of features?
Listen for: The action or process connecting them.

17–22 min · Worked example

Worked example · Landscape detectives

On screen: Name the physical and human features. / Explain an action linking people and nature.

Demonstrate this complete example: A reservoir contains water, but a dam built by people changes its storage. Name the natural feature, the human action and the effect; do not force every example into one box. Explain each operation or causal link aloud. Then give pupils the different case on the next step.

A farmer plants trees to shelter crops. Which explanation connects people and nature?

On screen:

Use the worked example’s method on this different case. Invite pupils’ reasoning before showing: People change vegetation to reduce wind exposure. Vegetation is natural material; planting and shelter are human action and purpose.

Class board challenge · Classify a feature and explain an interaction

On screen: Watch your teacher demonstrate one move. / One volunteer can come to the board; everyone else watches.

Introduce the rule before making a move. A reservoir contains water, but a dam built by people changes its storage. Name the natural feature, the human action and the effect; do not force every example into one box. Explain why one choice fits and why the other does not. Vegetation is natural material; planting and shelter are human action and purpose. Then invite a volunteer for one turn if useful. Take one brief response from the class and finish by restating the geographical idea. This is the one core board activity for this topic; the teacher may operate it throughout.

22–32 min · Student practice

Landscape detectives

On screen: Make three columns: physical, human, interaction. / Place five features and explain one overlap.

Pupils create labelled features and a connection diagram using the displayed evidence. Task: Make three columns: physical, human, interaction. Place five features and explain one overlap. Listen for: River and slope: physical; houses and bridge: human; clearing woodland changes habitat and runoff, an interaction. Allow independent work before comparing. Do not invent missing data. Accept different justified responses where the case allows them.

Check and improve your labelled features and a connection diagram

On screen: Name the physical and human features. / Explain an action linking people and nature. / Explain one correction or useful addition to your partner.

Partners compare their work with the evidence, not just each other’s answers. Check Name the physical and human features. Explain an action linking people and nature. Separate observations from predictions. In combined lessons, each partner chooses a different investigation. Keep the original response and explain one revision.

Share a result and explain it

On screen: Show one result from Landscape detectives. / Explain how the evidence supports it, using explain an action linking people and nature.

Invite two short explanations, preferably different methods or conclusions. Check each against its case source. Expected reasoning for the final case: River and slope: physical; houses and bridge: human; clearing woodland changes habitat and runoff, an interaction.

32–37 min · Check understanding

Explain one possible connection between them.

On screen:

Collect an independent explanation using this new source. Do not reveal until pupils have attempted it. Listen for: The proposed human action may change shade, infiltration or habitat. Describe the effect relevant to this source; it is a prediction until observations test it. Accept equivalent justified wording.

What could we observe to test the prediction?

On screen:

Collect an independent explanation using this new source. Do not reveal until pupils have attempted it. Listen for: Compare the affected area with a similar unchanged area; measure the predicted effect at comparable times. Accept equivalent justified wording.

37–40 min · Exit ticket and wrap-up

Exit ticket · Classify a feature and explain an interaction

On screen: Independently: A pupil says “human and physical geography never overlap”. Repair that claim.

Collect an independent response without a displayed model. Listen for: The footpath can affect the wooded slope; environmental questions study that connection. Use errors to choose the next recap.

Build a school geography exhibit / Pack the right kit

7A · Week 3 · sections 1.1, 1.2

40-minute route: recall 4, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 8, worked example 5, practice 10, check 5, exit 3. Divide each section between the topics in combined lessons. Timings are estimates.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

What are some ways we can ask questions about location?

On screen:

Invite pupils to suggest questions they could ask when finding a place at school. Use the illustration of two students asking for directions as a starting point. Accept questions about where something is, how to reach it, or its position relative to another place. Reveal the example questions after pupils have contributed.

Can a ruler tell us which way is north?

On screen:

Ask whether the ruler in the illustration can identify north. Invite answers before revealing: a ruler measures length; finding north needs a compass or a map’s north arrow. The picture deliberately shows no compass or north arrow.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can create a geography label for a place at school.

On screen: Example label · Shaded bench / A built seat beneath a tree. / Question: Is it cooler here at noon than on the sunny path? / Name and describe the feature. / Identify its physical and human features. / Ask a question we could investigate.

Introduce the exhibit as a display that helps visitors understand places at school. Point to the sample bench label: it names and describes a visible feature, brings together a human feature (the built seat) and a physical feature (the tree), and asks a question that observations or measurements could answer. Explain that the question is not a measured conclusion. Pupils will learn to create a label for a school feature. Keep this preview brief; teach the categories and the method in the following stages.

I can choose the right tool for a geography question.

On screen: Where is it? → Map / Which way is north? → Compass / How long is the line on the map? → Ruler / Say what information I need. / Choose a suitable tool. / Explain how the tool helps.

Link back to the opening questions about location and north. Point to the three resources: use a map to locate a place, a compass to find direction, and a ruler to measure a line. Distinguish measuring a line on the map from finding the real distance, which also needs the map scale. Preview the goal: pupils should explain their choice using the information the tool provides. Keep the questions within the school context.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for describing school places

On screen: Physical geography: Natural features and processes: soil, plants and rain. / Human geography: People and their activities: building paths and using benches. / Interaction: People and nature affect each other: people water plants.

Read each term and point to a concrete example. Soil and plants are natural materials; building and using paths are human activities. The watering picture shows an interaction. A planted garden contains both natural features and human actions. Invite pupils to name one feature at school; accept equivalent explanations rather than forcing every place into one category.

Words for using geography tools

On screen: Map: A drawing of a place from above. Use it to locate features. / Compass: A tool for finding direction. Its magnetic needle helps find north. / Scale: Links map distance to ground distance: 1 cm can represent 10 m.

Introduce map, compass and scale with their individual pictures. An atlas is a collection of maps. Point to north on the compass diagram and to the repeated ten-metre sections on the scale diagram. A ruler measures the map line; it needs the map scale to give ground distance. These diagrams use printed example values, not the physical size of the screen.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Start with what you can see

On screen: A wooden bench stands beneath a tree. / “This is the coolest place” needs temperature evidence.

Point to the bench, tree and shade. The picture supports descriptions of visible features, not a measured temperature claim. Model the difference between an observation and a claim needing evidence. Invite one additional visible detail.

Brief check: What can the picture tell us without a thermometer?
Listen for: A bench is beneath a tree, with visible shade.

A place can have physical and human features

On screen: Physical: the tree, plants and soil. / Human: the built bench and paved path.

Identify the natural materials and the things people built or do here. A tree can be planted by people and still be a natural living feature. Categories describe different aspects of the same place; do not force the whole scene into one box.

Brief check: Can a school garden involve both?
Listen for: Yes. Plants and soil are natural; planting and watering are human activities.

Explain how people and nature connect

On screen: The tree shades a place where people sit. / People plant and water the garden.

Explain two directions of interaction. Nature affects people when a tree provides shade. People affect nature through planting and watering. Ask pupils to explain an action rather than list two nouns. Do not claim measured growth or temperature from artwork.

Brief check: How do people affect the plants in this picture?
Listen for: They water the plants and care for the garden.

Turn a description into a question

On screen: Description: a bench beneath a tree. / Question: Is it cooler here than on the sunny path?

Explain that a label can describe a place and invite an investigation. The question names two places and something measurable: temperature. “Is the bench nice?” needs clarification about what nice means. Preview a same-time comparison with a thermometer; keep the answer open until observations exist.

Brief check: What would help answer the temperature question?
Listen for: Temperature readings at the bench and sunny path, taken at the same time.

Start with the question, then choose a tool

On screen: Where is it? → Map / Which way is north? → Compass

Connect directly to the opening questions. A map gives relative locations; a compass helps find direction. A ruler measures length. A north arrow on a map also supplies a directional reference. A photograph helps describe appearance but does not provide an exact ground distance by itself.

Brief check: Can the ruler alone find north?
Listen for: No. It measures length; north needs a directional reference.

Read the map before giving directions

On screen: Find the named places and the north arrow. / The bench is north of the gate; the school is east of the bench.

Point to the gate, bench, school and arrow on this fictional map. Trace the vertical path up from the gate, then the horizontal path toward the school. Name the starting place when giving directions. The colours show grass, paths and built features; the text identifies the places.

Brief check: From the bench, which way is the school?
Listen for: East.

Use the ruler and the scale together

On screen: Bench → school: 3 cm on the map. / At 1 cm = 10 m: 3 × 10 m = 30 m.

Model starting at the ruler’s zero mark, reading centimetres, then checking the map scale. Show three equal ten-metre sections. Distinguish map centimetres from ground metres. The drawing is schematic: use its printed values, not a ruler against the board.

Brief check: Why do we multiply 3 by 10?
Listen for: Each of the three map centimetres represents another ten metres.

Record enough information to check

On screen: Map line: bench → school, 3 cm. / Ground distance: 30 m, using the scale 1 cm = 10 m.

Compare “It is 30” with a record naming the path, result, unit and source. A visitor needs to know what the number describes. For other investigations, also record where and when observations were made. Do not invent field measurements.

Brief check: What is missing from “It is 30”?
Listen for: The feature, unit and method or source.

17–22 min · Worked example

Build a label: name, describe, ask

On screen: Shaded bench: a wooden seat beneath a tree. / Physical: tree. Human: built seat. / Question: Is it cooler here at noon than on the sunny path?

Write the label aloud in three parts. Name and describe the feature; identify its physical and human aspects; add a question measurements could answer. Explain that the question is a plan, not a claim that the bench is cooler. This is the model for the labels pupils will create.

How could we answer the bench question?

On screen: Choose a tool and explain what you would compare.

Invite a suggestion before revealing. A compass, map or ruler does not measure temperature. Compare temperatures at the shaded bench and sunny path at the same time. Repeat on other days before making a general claim. Demonstrate choosing the tool from the information needed, rather than restricting pupils to the three map tools.

Worked route: gate → bench → school

On screen: Walk north from the gate to the bench. / Then walk east to the school. / Map route: 4 + 3 = 7 cm. Ground route: 7 × 10 m = 70 m.

Trace each named part of the route. First use the north arrow for direction, then add the two labelled map lengths and apply the scale. Distinguish the total route of seventy metres from the bench-to-school leg of thirty metres. Ask a pupil to explain one step.

What needs improving in this label?

On screen: “School garden: the best garden in the world.” / Improve it with a description and a question.

Collect suggestions before revealing. Accept other descriptions and checkable questions tied to the garden. Explain that “best” lacks a clear measure. If pupils ask about plant growth, they would record changes over time; one picture cannot establish the result.

22–32 min · Student practice

Create three labels for your exhibit

On screen: Choose three school features, or use the bench, garden and path. / For each: name it, describe it, identify physical or human features. / Add one question you could investigate.

Allow four minutes of independent writing in exercise books. Sketches are optional. Accept short labels and equivalent English. Pupils can use remembered school details or clearly identify the supplied examples as imagined places. Do not require leaving the classroom. Look for specific descriptions and questions rather than guesses presented as facts.

Choose evidence for one of your questions

On screen: Pick one label. Say what you need to find out. / Choose a tool and explain how you would use it. / Record the place, result and unit where needed.

Allow three minutes. Pupils plan an investigation; they do not need to take real measurements today. Match temperature to a thermometer, length to a ruler and scale, direction to a compass or north arrow, and appearance to observation or a photograph. Counting may need a tally rather than an instrument. Ask pupils to avoid invented results.

Check and improve your labels

On screen: Read one label to a partner. / Check: clear description, physical or human features, checkable question. / Improve one unclear sentence or tool choice.

Allow two minutes for a concrete peer check. Each pupil keeps their own work and revises one part. A partner should explain why a question can be answered and whether the proposed tool supplies the information. Support pupils who need help by returning to the bench example.

Share one label and its investigation plan

On screen: Read one label to the class. / Explain which evidence or tool would answer its question.

Invite one or two brief examples within one minute. Ask the class to identify the description, question and evidence plan. Keep unanswered questions open; do not invent investigation results.

32–37 min · Check understanding

Create a label for this school path

On screen: Name a visible feature and its physical or human aspect. / Add an investigation question and explain how to answer it.

Give pupils an independent response before revealing. Accept other visible descriptions and suitable questions. The picture shows a puddle; it does not prove when rain fell or compare drainage rates. Listen for description, category, checkable question and an appropriate evidence plan. Record observations of the path and nearby soil at the same times after rain.

Help a visitor get from the gate to the bench

On screen: Which direction should they walk? / How far is it on the ground? Explain your method.

Ask pupils to work independently. This uses a different distance from the seventy-metre teacher route. Check both direction and conversion with units. If a pupil gives seventy metres, ask where that longer route ends. Reveal after collecting explanations.

37–40 min · Exit ticket and wrap-up

Exit ticket: a new place, a new question

On screen: Independently choose a school feature you have not labelled yet. / Write a description and a question we could investigate. / Name the evidence or tool you would use, and explain why.

Allow two minutes independently, without displaying a model answer. Collect the response or hear a small sample. Look for a specific feature, an evidence-based description, a checkable question and a suitable method. Use the responses to choose the next recap.

Rescue the survey team / Three equipment stations

7A · Week 4 · sections 1.2, 1.2

40-minute route: recall 4, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 8, worked example 5, practice 10, check 5, exit 3. Divide each section between the topics in combined lessons. Timings are estimates.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

Can a ruler tell us which way is north?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. No. Use a compass or a map’s north arrow; a ruler measures length. Connect this to today’s task: Three equipment stations.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can repair an incorrect measurement method.

On screen: Today’s task: Rescue the survey team / You will make a tool-and-result record. / Match the tool to the information needed. / Use the scale for real distance. / Record the feature, result and unit.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: a tool-and-result record. Explain the three criteria: Match the tool to the information needed. Use the scale for real distance. Record the feature, result and unit. The independent task uses this case: A team used a photograph to claim a path is 500 m long and a ruler to find north. The map says 1 cm = 50 m; the path is 6 cm.

I can record a result another investigator can check.

On screen: Today’s task: Three equipment stations / You will make a tool-and-result record. / Match the tool to the information needed. / Use the scale for real distance. / Record the feature, result and unit.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: a tool-and-result record. Explain the three criteria: Match the tool to the information needed. Use the scale for real distance. Record the feature, result and unit. The independent task uses this case: Mini atlas index: Brazil—South America; China—East Asia; Ireland—west of Great Britain. Map line A is labelled 7 cm. Classroom observation: choose a visible feature.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Atlas: A collection of maps. An atlas index helps locate Brazil. / Compass: A tool that shows direction. A compass helps find north. / Scale: The link between map and real distance. At 1 cm = 10 m, 3 cm represents 30 m.

Atlas: A collection of maps. Example: An atlas index helps locate Brazil. Compass: A tool that shows direction. Example: A compass helps find north. Scale: The link between map and real distance. Example: At 1 cm = 10 m, 3 cm represents 30 m. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Match a tool to a question

On screen: Location: map or atlas. / Direction: north arrow or compass.

Begin with the question before choosing a tool. An atlas contains maps and an index that helps us find places. A compass helps identify direction. A ruler measures a line, but does not tell us which country we are looking at. Show how the same place can be investigated in several ways. To locate it, use a map; to describe its appearance, use a photograph; to estimate a mapped distance, use a ruler and the map scale. No single tool answers every geographical question.

Brief check: Can a ruler tell us which way is north?
Listen for: No. A ruler measures length; direction needs another reference.

Read a map carefully

On screen: Find the title, key and north arrow. / Check the scale before measuring.

A map is a selective drawing of a place. Its title tells us the area or topic. The key explains symbols and colours. The north arrow gives direction, and the scale connects the drawing to real distances. Demonstrate this order before identifying individual features. A blue line might represent a river, but we should confirm it using the key. A large symbol may be easy to see without showing the feature’s exact size. Reading the supporting information prevents us from guessing from appearance alone.

Brief check: Why should we read the key?
Listen for: It tells us what this map’s symbols mean.

Measure and convert

On screen: Start at the ruler’s zero mark. / Map length × scale = ground distance.

Place the zero mark at the start of the line, not the edge of the ruler. State the map measurement in centimetres. If the scale says one centimetre represents forty metres, each centimetre is one equal forty-metre section. A three-centimetre path represents three times forty, or one hundred and twenty metres. The units change because we move from the drawing to the ground. Adding three and forty would mix different quantities. Show the three equal sections before writing the multiplication.

Brief check: Why do we multiply rather than add?
Listen for: Each map centimetre represents another equal section of ground distance.

Record a result others can check

On screen: Name the feature, result and unit. / Say which tool or source you used.

“It is four” is not a complete geographical record. We do not know what was measured or what four means. “Path B measures four centimetres on this map” identifies the object, number and unit. Add the scale when calculating the ground distance. A photograph also needs a place and date if it is used to show change. Clear records let another person check the method instead of trusting an unexplained answer. Model a weak record and improve it aloud, keeping the original visible for comparison.

Brief check: What information is missing from “It is four”?

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Observation and inference

On screen: Observation: what we can see or measure. / Inference: a possible explanation.

An observation comes from a source or measurement. If a photograph shows a queue, we can describe the people visible. Saying that everyone likes the shop is an inference: it suggests a reason that the photograph does not establish. Other reasons are possible, such as slow service or a special event. Use a familiar classroom example before returning to the geographical image. Keep observations and proposed explanations in different columns. This allows pupils to offer ideas while still understanding which claims have actually been checked.

Brief check: Does a long queue prove a shop is popular?
Listen for: No. Popularity is one possible explanation; other reasons could produce a queue.

Make a question measurable

On screen: Choose one place or feature. / Decide what you will count or measure.

“Is our school good?” is too broad for a simple geographical enquiry. “How many people use each gate in five minutes?” tells us what to observe, where and for how long. Explain how a count differs from an opinion. We can count people crossing a line, but happiness requires a different kind of evidence. A good question helps us choose an appropriate method. Before starting, agree exactly what counts as an entry so two observers would make comparable records.

Brief check: Which is easier to investigate: “good school” or “people using each gate”?
Listen for: The gate question gives a clear, countable outcome.

Make comparisons fair

On screen: Use the same counting time. / Use the same rule at each place.

Suppose we count one gate for five minutes and another for ten. The second may have a larger count because we watched longer, not because it is busier. Hold the counting time constant. We also need the same rule for entering and leaving, and comparable observation times. A bag on the boundary between two survey areas should be counted according to one agreed rule. Fairness here means controlling the method so the difference we report is meaningful. It is not about making all results equal.

Brief check: Why could different counting times mislead us?
Listen for: The longer observation has more opportunity to record people.

Repeat before making a broad claim

On screen: A count describes one time. / Repeated counts can reveal variation.

One count is a snapshot. A gate that is busy on Monday may be quieter on Tuesday. Show two days with different results and calculate the combined counts. Discuss why weather, events or lesson times might affect movement, without claiming we know the cause. Repeating a measurement makes us less dependent on one unusual moment. Even repeated counts at two gates do not automatically describe every entrance or every season. A conclusion should name the places and times studied and explain what remains unknown.

Brief check: Does one busy morning prove a gate is always busiest?
Listen for: No. We need comparable repeated observations.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Geography asks about places

On screen: What is here? Where is it? / Why is it here? How does it affect people?

Geography helps us understand places and the connections between them. Start with our classroom. The building has a location, people use it, and its surroundings influence how we reach it. Now move out to the school, the town and the world. These are different scales of study. A question about one street needs local detail; a question about countries needs a wider view. Geography joins information about nature and people rather than treating a place as a list of names.

Brief check: Which question asks about location?
Listen for: “Where is it?” asks about location.

Explain a connection

On screen: Name the feature and the change. / Use “because” or “so”.

Compare two sentences. “River, bridge, school” lists three features. “The bridge crosses the river, so pupils can reach the school from the other bank” explains a connection. Point to each feature while saying its part of the sentence. The word so joins an action to an effect. Because introduces a reason. A useful geographical explanation tells us how the connection works. “The bridge is good” gives a judgement without explaining it. Ask the class which words show what the bridge actually does.

Brief check: What is missing from a list of features?
Listen for: The action or process connecting them.

Match a tool to a question

On screen: Location: map or atlas. / Direction: north arrow or compass.

Begin with the question before choosing a tool. An atlas contains maps and an index that helps us find places. A compass helps identify direction. A ruler measures a line, but does not tell us which country we are looking at. Show how the same place can be investigated in several ways. To locate it, use a map; to describe its appearance, use a photograph; to estimate a mapped distance, use a ruler and the map scale. No single tool answers every geographical question.

Brief check: Can a ruler tell us which way is north?
Listen for: No. A ruler measures length; direction needs another reference.

Record a result others can check

On screen: Name the feature, result and unit. / Say which tool or source you used.

“It is four” is not a complete geographical record. We do not know what was measured or what four means. “Path B measures four centimetres on this map” identifies the object, number and unit. Add the scale when calculating the ground distance. A photograph also needs a place and date if it is used to show change. Clear records let another person check the method instead of trusting an unexplained answer. Model a weak record and improve it aloud, keeping the original visible for comparison.

Brief check: What information is missing from “It is four”?
Listen for: The feature, unit and method are missing.

This allows pupils to offer ideas while still understanding which claims have actually been checked.

Words for today

On screen: Observation: Something you see or measure. Eight pupils wait at Door A. / Evidence: Information supporting an answer. A timed count supports a queue comparison. / Enquiry: A question investigated with evidence. Do the queues differ at the same time each day?

Observation: Something you see or measure. Example: Eight pupils wait at Door A. Evidence: Information supporting an answer. Example: A timed count supports a queue comparison. Enquiry: A question investigated with evidence. Example: Do the queues differ at the same time each day? Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

Land use: How people use an area. Example: Fields can become housing. Industry: Making goods and providing services. Example: Workshops make or repair goods. Change: A difference between two times. Example: A ferry crossing is replaced by a bridge. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. 9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Observation and inference

On screen: Observation: what we can see or measure. / Inference: a possible explanation.

An observation comes from a source or measurement. If a photograph shows a queue, we can describe the people visible. Saying that everyone likes the shop is an inference: it suggests a reason that the photograph does not establish. Other reasons are possible, such as slow service or a special event. Use a familiar classroom example before returning to the geographical image. Keep observations and proposed explanations in different columns. This allows pupils to offer ideas while still understanding which claims have actually been checked.

Brief check: Does a long queue prove a shop is popular?
Listen for: No. Popularity is one possible explanation; other reasons could produce a queue.

Make a question measurable

On screen: Choose one place or feature. / Decide what you will count or measure.

“Is our school good?” is too broad for a simple geographical enquiry. “How many people use each gate in five minutes?” tells us what to observe, where and for how long. Explain how a count differs from an opinion. We can count people crossing a line, but happiness requires a different kind of evidence. A good question helps us choose an appropriate method. Before starting, agree exactly what counts as an entry so two observers would make comparable records.

Brief check: Which is easier to investigate: “good school” or “people using each gate”?
Listen for: The gate question gives a clear, countable outcome.

Make comparisons fair

On screen: Use the same counting time. / Use the same rule at each place.

Suppose we count one gate for five minutes and another for ten. The second may have a larger count because we watched longer, not because it is busier. Hold the counting time constant. We also need the same rule for entering and leaving, and comparable observation times. A bag on the boundary between two survey areas should be counted according to one agreed rule. Fairness here means controlling the method so the difference we report is meaningful. It is not about making all results equal.

Brief check: Why could different counting times mislead us?
Listen for: The longer observation has more opportunity to record people.

Repeat before making a broad claim

On screen: A count describes one time. / Repeated counts can reveal variation.

One count is a snapshot. A gate that is busy on Monday may be quieter on Tuesday. Show two days with different results and calculate the combined counts. Discuss why weather, events or lesson times might affect movement, without claiming we know the cause. Repeating a measurement makes us less dependent on one unusual moment. Even repeated counts at two gates do not automatically describe every entrance or every season. A conclusion should name the places and times studied and explain what remains unknown.

Brief check: Does one busy morning prove a gate is always busiest?
Listen for: No. We need comparable repeated observations.

Ironbridge Gorge: a changing industrial landscape

On screen: Ironbridge Gorge is in Shropshire, beside the River Severn. / Industry, transport and settlement changed the landscape.

Ironbridge Gorge is a real place in Shropshire associated with the Industrial Revolution. The River Severn runs through the gorge. Its historic industrial landscape includes evidence of manufacturing, transport and homes, while the iron bridge is an important example of early large-scale structural use of cast iron. Explain why this is more than a story about one bridge: industry changes land use, creates connections between workplaces and housing, and leaves material traces. Today, historical remains can also serve heritage and visitor purposes. Use this factual background to introduce change, while keeping our imagined before-and-after drawings separate from verified historical records. We can practise comparison with a schematic, but cannot use invented building counts to describe the actual gorge’s history.

Brief check: Why should the fictional drawing’s counts not become historical Ironbridge facts?
Listen for: They are classroom data rather than historical records.

Places change over time

On screen: Look at the same place on two dates. / Separate what stayed from what changed.

A place can change in its buildings, transport, land use and environment. Put two views of the same place side by side. Start with a feature that appears in both so pupils know they are comparing the same area. Then identify a feature added, removed or altered. A stayed-and-changed table prevents us from treating the whole place as new. Dates matter: an undated photograph can show appearance, but cannot reliably establish which view came first. Keep imagined classroom scenes separate from verified historical photographs.

Brief check: Why do the dates matter?
Listen for: They establish the order of the changes.

A crossing changes access

On screen: A ferry crosses water in separate trips. / A bridge provides a fixed crossing when open.

A river can connect places by water while also making travel between its banks difficult. A ferry carries people or goods in trips. A bridge creates a fixed crossing, but it still needs suitable access and can close. Trace a journey before and after a crossing is added. Explain the mechanism: a shorter or more reliable route may make a destination easier to reach. We should not leap from a bridge symbol to a precise claim about jobs or income; those require separate records.

Brief check: What can a new crossing change directly?
Listen for: The routes people can use to move between the banks.

Describe first, explain second

On screen: “A workshop appeared” describes change. / “Access may have helped” suggests a cause.

Descriptions tell us what differs between the sources. Explanations suggest why that difference occurred. A new workshop beside a bridge may lead us to ask whether improved access helped the business. Its location alone does not prove that cause. The workshop might have opened for another reason or before the bridge. Demonstrate both sentence types using the same image. Accurate description is the starting point; a causal explanation needs evidence linking the change in transport to the change in activity.

Brief check: Does being close to a bridge prove a business opened because of it?
Listen for: No. Location alone does not establish cause.

Test the proposed cause

On screen: A cause must come before its effect. / Use dates, records and comparisons.

If a shop opened in 2015 and the bridge opened in 2020, the bridge cannot explain the shop’s original opening. It could still affect later customer numbers. Split those two claims rather than accepting or rejecting everything at once. To investigate later effects, compare suitable records before and after the crossing, and consider other changes. This is how historical geography joins the story of a place to evidence. A convincing explanation identifies a possible mechanism and checks whether the timing and records support it.

Brief check: What does an earlier shop opening rule out?
Listen for: The later bridge cannot have caused that original opening.

Words for today

On screen: Identify: Name the feature. Name the crossing: bridge. / Describe: Say what it is like. Six homes near it; two farther away. / Explain: Give a reason and connect ideas. The crossing may make travel easier.

Identify: Name the feature. Example: Name the crossing: bridge. Describe: Say what it is like. Example: Six homes near it; two farther away. Explain: Give a reason and connect ideas. Example: The crossing may make travel easier. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. 9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Identify means name

On screen: Give the requested feature. / Use the correct geographical term.

Command words tell us what kind of answer is needed. Identify means name or recognise. If the question asks us to identify the crossing, “footbridge” may be sufficient. A long story about why people need transport answers a different question. Point to the feature before naming it so pupils link the term to the visual. If several crossings are shown, add enough location information to distinguish the requested one. Accuracy comes before length: a short relevant answer can be better than a long unrelated one.

Brief check: Does “people travel faster” identify a crossing?
Listen for: No. It explains a possible effect rather than naming the feature.

Describe means say what it is like

On screen: Use position, shape and number. / Describe the visible pattern.

To describe a settlement, say where its buildings lie and how they are arranged. “Six homes are beside the bridge and two are farther away” gives a count and location. “People want jobs” is a possible explanation, not a description of the visible pattern. Move a finger across the image as you describe it so pupils can match each phrase to evidence. Useful description words include near, beside, north of, scattered and clustered. The relevant words depend on the feature being studied.

Brief check: Which adds detail: “some homes” or “six homes beside the bridge”?

Explain means give the connection

On screen: Give a reason or process. / Show how it leads to the result.

An explanation needs more than the word because. “The homes are here because they are here” adds no cause. “A crossing may improve access, so people may choose nearby homes” supplies a mechanism. The explanation should remain connected to the actual place or source in the question rather than becoming a memorised sentence about any settlement.

On screen: Find the command word. / Then find the place and evidence required.

Read a question in three parts: what to do, which feature or place, and which source to use. A pupil may know a correct fact but still fail to answer the question. Show a deliberate mismatch, such as a cause given when the question asks for a pattern. Repair the response by keeping any useful detail and replacing the irrelevant part. This is a method pupils can apply across Geography. A good answer is relevant, accurate and supported; its length depends on the task rather than on filling space.

Brief check: What should we check before adding more sentences?

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Identify means name

On screen: Give the requested feature. / Use the correct geographical term.

Command words tell us what kind of answer is needed. Identify means name or recognise. If the question asks us to identify the crossing, “footbridge” may be sufficient. A long story about why people need transport answers a different question. Point to the feature before naming it so pupils link the term to the visual. If several crossings are shown, add enough location information to distinguish the requested one. Accuracy comes before length: a short relevant answer can be better than a long unrelated one.

Brief check: Does “people travel faster” identify a crossing?
Listen for: No. It explains a possible effect rather than naming the feature.

Describe means say what it is like

On screen: Use position, shape and number. / Describe the visible pattern.

To describe a settlement, say where its buildings lie and how they are arranged. “Six homes are beside the bridge and two are farther away” gives a count and location. “People want jobs” is a possible explanation, not a description of the visible pattern. Move a finger across the image as you describe it so pupils can match each phrase to evidence. Useful description words include near, beside, north of, scattered and clustered. The relevant words depend on the feature being studied.

Brief check: Which adds detail: “some homes” or “six homes beside the bridge”?
Listen for: The second gives both number and location.

Explain means give the connection

On screen: Give a reason or process. / Show how it leads to the result.

An explanation needs more than the word because. “The homes are here because they are here” adds no cause. “A crossing may improve access, so people may choose nearby homes” supplies a mechanism. When the source shows only a pattern, use cautious language rather than pretending the cause was measured. Explain by tracing the sequence: crossing, easier access, possible location choice. The explanation should remain connected to the actual place or source in the question rather than becoming a memorised sentence about any settlement.

Brief check: What makes an explanation useful?
Listen for: It connects a reason or process to the result.

Answer the question asked

On screen: Find the command word. / Then find the place and evidence required.

Read a question in three parts: what to do, which feature or place, and which source to use. A pupil may know a correct fact but still fail to answer the question. Show a deliberate mismatch, such as a cause given when the question asks for a pattern. Repair the response by keeping any useful detail and replacing the irrelevant part. This is a method pupils can apply across Geography. A good answer is relevant, accurate and supported; its length depends on the task rather than on filling space.

Brief check: What should we check before adding more sentences?
Listen for: Whether the answer matches the command word and requested feature.

A claim needs support

On screen: Claim: what you say is true. / Evidence: the detail that supports it.

A claim states an idea about a place. Evidence is the observation, count or source detail we use to support that idea. “Shops cluster near the stop” is a claim. “Twelve of sixteen shops are within two hundred metres” makes the pattern more precise. Explain that evidence must be relevant: the colour of a shop sign does not test a claim about customer transport. We should be able to point to the supporting information and explain why it bears on the claim.

Brief check: Which supports clustering: a shop colour or a count with distance?
Listen for: The count and distance are relevant to the pattern.

Join evidence to the explanation

On screen: Say what the detail shows. / Explain why it matters.

A number does not explain itself. After giving a count, say what it tells us about the distribution. Then separate that pattern from a proposed cause. Many shops near a bus stop may be consistent with customers valuing access, but the count alone does not show why each business opened. Use two arrows: count to pattern, then possible access mechanism to explanation. The first can be directly supported by the count; the second needs more information about customers or business decisions.

Brief check: Can a location count tell us every business owner’s reason?
Listen for: No. It establishes the pattern, not every cause.

Ask for relevant new evidence

On screen: Customer survey: how did you travel? / Business records: when did the shop open?

The best next source depends on the claim being tested. If we want to know whether a bus stop brings customers, ask customers about travel and reasons for visiting. If we want to know whether the stop caused shops to open, compare opening dates and the stop’s history. Different questions need different evidence. More information is useful only if it addresses the uncertainty. Demonstrate a relevant and an irrelevant question, then explain why the relevant one could change our confidence in the proposed connection.

Brief check: Which evidence tests original opening: paint colour or dates?
Listen for: Dates can test whether the proposed cause came first.

State a useful limit

On screen: Say what is supported. / Say what still needs checking.

A limitation is a boundary on what we can conclude. It does not mean the investigation was worthless. We may accurately report that shops cluster in our mapped area while admitting that we did not measure the reasons for their location. Avoid extremes such as “we know everything” or “we know nothing”. Model a balanced conclusion: the source supports this pattern, a mechanism may explain it, and this further evidence would test that mechanism. Changing a claim when new evidence appears is part of good geographical reasoning.

Brief check: Does recognising a limit make all the evidence useless?
Listen for: No. Keep the supported finding and qualify the uncertain part.

Ironbridge Gorge: a changing industrial landscape

On screen: Ironbridge Gorge is in Shropshire, beside the River Severn. / Industry, transport and settlement changed the landscape.

Ironbridge Gorge is a real place in Shropshire associated with the Industrial Revolution. The River Severn runs through the gorge. Its historic industrial landscape includes evidence of manufacturing, transport and homes, while the iron bridge is an important example of early large-scale structural use of cast iron. Explain why this is more than a story about one bridge: industry changes land use, creates connections between workplaces and housing, and leaves material traces. Today, historical remains can also serve heritage and visitor purposes. Use this factual background to introduce change, while keeping our imagined before-and-after drawings separate from verified historical records. We can practise comparison with a schematic, but cannot use invented building counts to describe the actual gorge’s history.

On screen: A cause must come before its effect. / Use dates, records and comparisons.

Split those two claims rather than accepting or rejecting everything at once. To investigate later effects, compare suitable records before and after the crossing, and consider other changes. This is how historical geography joins the story of a place to evidence. A convincing explanation identifies a possible mechanism and checks whether the timing and records support it.

Brief check: What does an earlier shop opening rule out?

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Claim: A statement to support or test. Most listed shops are near the stop. / Evidence: Information supporting a claim. Twelve shops within 200 m; three farther away. / Reasoning: How evidence supports an answer. Access may help; the counts do not prove why.

Claim: A statement to support or test. Example: Most listed shops are near the stop. Evidence: Information supporting a claim. Example: Twelve shops within 200 m; three farther away. 9–17 min · Teacher explanation

A claim needs support

On screen: Claim: what you say is true. / Evidence: the detail that supports it.

A claim states an idea about a place. Evidence is the observation, count or source detail we use to support that idea. “Shops cluster near the stop” is a claim. “Twelve of sixteen shops are within two hundred metres” makes the pattern more precise. Explain that evidence must be relevant: the colour of a shop sign does not test a claim about customer transport. We should be able to point to the supporting information and explain why it bears on the claim.

Brief check: Which supports clustering: a shop colour or a count with distance?
Listen for: The count and distance are relevant to the pattern.

Join evidence to the explanation

On screen: Say what the detail shows. / Explain why it matters.

A number does not explain itself. After giving a count, say what it tells us about the distribution. Then separate that pattern from a proposed cause. Many shops near a bus stop may be consistent with customers valuing access, but the count alone does not show why each business opened. Use two arrows: count to pattern, then possible access mechanism to explanation. The first can be directly supported by the count; the second needs more information about customers or business decisions.

Brief check: Can a location count tell us every business owner’s reason?
Listen for: No. It establishes the pattern, not every cause.

Ask for relevant new evidence

On screen: Customer survey: how did you travel? / Business records: when did the shop open?

The best next source depends on the claim being tested. If we want to know whether a bus stop brings customers, ask customers about travel and reasons for visiting. If we want to know whether the stop caused shops to open, compare opening dates and the stop’s history. Different questions need different evidence. More information is useful only if it addresses the uncertainty. Demonstrate a relevant and an irrelevant question, then explain why the relevant one could change our confidence in the proposed connection.

Brief check: Which evidence tests original opening: paint colour or dates?
Listen for: Dates can test whether the proposed cause came first.

State a useful limit

On screen: Say what is supported. / Say what still needs checking.

A limitation is a boundary on what we can conclude. It does not mean the investigation was worthless. We may accurately report that shops cluster in our mapped area while admitting that we did not measure the reasons for their location. Avoid extremes such as “we know everything” or “we know nothing”. Model a balanced conclusion: the source supports this pattern, a mechanism may explain it, and this further evidence would test that mechanism. Changing a claim when new evidence appears is part of good geographical reasoning.

Brief check: Does recognising a limit make all the evidence useless?
Listen for: No. Keep the supported finding and qualify the uncertain part.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

Must the shortest route be the best for every traveller?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. No. Access, closures and safety may matter more for a particular traveller. Connect this to today’s task: Change the traveller.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can evaluate a route for a named traveller.

On screen: Today’s task: Choose for a traveller / You will make a justified route recommendation. / Compare distance using the same units. / Check access and whether the route is open. / Explain the choice and one condition to check.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: a justified route recommendation. Explain the three criteria: Compare distance using the same units. Check access and whether the route is open. Explain the choice and one condition to check. The independent task uses this case: Route A: 400 m with stairs. Route B: 600 m with a ramp. The traveller uses a wheelchair.

I can change the criteria when the user changes.

On screen: Today’s task: Change the traveller / You will make a justified route recommendation. / Compare distance using the same units. / Check access and whether the route is open. / Explain the choice and one condition to check.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: a justified route recommendation. Explain the three criteria: Compare distance using the same units. Check access and whether the route is open. Explain the choice and one condition to check. The independent task uses this case: A walker has no difficulty with stairs and wants the shortest route. Use the same A/B routes.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Route: A path linking a start and destination. School → library → market. / Constraint: A condition a plan must meet. A closed route cannot be used today. / Preference: Something a person would like. A walker may prefer the shortest open route.

Route: A path linking a start and destination. Example: School → library → market. Constraint: A condition a plan must meet. Example: A closed route cannot be used today. Preference: Something a person would like. Example: A walker may prefer the shortest open route. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Routes connect a start and destination

On screen: Trace every section in order. / A straight line may not be a usable route.

A route is a sequence of connected sections between places. Trace the start, crossings, turns and destination. A straight line may be shorter on a map but could cross a fence, river or private land. The route must be usable by the traveller. Explain why geography considers the arrangement of places and the connections between them. Looking at distance alone ignores how the journey actually works. Before comparing routes, make sure each one begins and ends at the required locations and has no missing connection.

Brief check: Why might the straight line fail?
Listen for: It may cross a barrier or an inaccessible area.

Different travellers have different needs

On screen: Stairs can be a barrier. / Surface and slope affect access.

Imagine a traveller using a wheelchair and another walking without luggage. A staircase shortcut may work for one and prevent the other from travelling. A ramp label helps, but its gradient, width and surface condition still matter. Accessibility is a practical question about whether this person can use this route. It is not a judgement that one traveller is better than another. Point to the obstacle and explain its effect before comparing convenience. The shortest route may fail a necessary access condition.

Brief check: Should we choose stairs for every traveller because they are shorter?
Listen for: No. Check whether the traveller can use them.

Constraints and preferences

On screen: Constraint: a condition that must be met. / Preference: something we would like.

A constraint rules out a route when a required condition fails. A closed gate or unusable staircase can stop a journey. A preference helps choose between routes that work, such as a shorter distance or quieter surroundings. Establish feasibility before choosing favourites. Show a short closed route and a longer open route. The closed one cannot become feasible simply because we prefer it. This order makes a recommendation clear: first explain why the route can be used, then explain why it is the preferred usable option.

Brief check: Is an open route a preference or a necessary condition?
Listen for: Availability is a necessary condition.

Revise when conditions change

On screen: A closure can change the best route. / Check current conditions before travelling.

Maps describe locations and selected features, but they may not include a closure that happened this morning. A route that was suitable yesterday may be unavailable today. Show the old recommendation, add one changed condition and reconsider it aloud. Keep unchanged facts, such as the destination, while revising the affected route. Ask what information is needed before using an alternative: surface, crossing, opening hours or other relevant conditions. A good decision responds to evidence rather than defending an answer after its conditions have failed.

Brief check: What should happen to a recommendation after a route closes?
Listen for: Check alternatives and revise the route.

On screen: Compare distance using the same units. / Check access and whether the route is open.

For a wheelchair user, usable access is a constraint, while distance is a preference after access is checked. A ramp still needs a suitable gradient and condition. Explain each operation or causal link aloud. Then give pupils the different case on the next step.

Maps describe locations and selected features, but they may not include a closure that happened this morning. A route that was suitable yesterday may be unavailable today. Show the old recommendation, add one changed condition and reconsider it aloud. Keep unchanged facts, such as the destination, while revising the affected route. Ask what information is needed before using an alternative: surface, crossing, opening hours or other relevant conditions. A good decision responds to evidence rather than defending an answer after its conditions have failed.

Brief check: What should happen to a recommendation after a route closes?
Listen for: Check alternatives and revise the route.

Map making has developed

On screen: Surveying improved position and distance information. / Digital maps combine data in changeable layers.

Maps have been made for navigation, ownership, government, exploration and many other purposes. Their development is not simply a move from bad pictures to good ones. Different maps serve different needs. Surveying methods improved the measurement of positions and distances; printing helped reproduce maps; aerial and satellite observations supplied further information. Digital systems can combine layers and update selected data. A satellite image is still not identical to a road map: it records visible information that must be interpreted and combined with other sources. Explain what each development makes possible, then keep the key questions unchanged: who made the map, for what purpose, at what date and scale? Technology can improve the information available without making every map complete or suitable for every journey.

Brief check: Is a satellite image automatically the same as a usable road map?
Listen for: No. A road map selects and explains information for a particular purpose.

A map has a purpose

On screen: Maps select information. / Different users need different detail.

A map represents selected information about a place. A road map helps drivers see routes; a historical map may show former buildings or industries; a weather map presents a different kind of information. No map can display every detail clearly at once. Ask who will use the map and which question it should answer. The omission of a feature may reflect the purpose or scale, rather than proving that the feature does not exist. Start by reading the title instead of treating every map as a complete picture.

Brief check: Does an absent symbol always prove a feature is absent on the ground?
Listen for: No. The map may omit it.

Direction needs a reference

On screen: Use the north arrow. / East and west are opposite directions.

On a north-up map, north is towards the top and east towards the right. However, a rotated map changes screen positions without changing real directions. Point to the north arrow first, then identify east, south and west relative to it. Use a route between two features to demonstrate a directional sentence. Direction describes one place relative to another, so reversing the journey can reverse the description. Do not use left and right as substitutes for compass directions unless the reference is clear.

Brief check: If we rotate a map, does the town move to a new real location?
Listen for: No. The view changes; the location does not.

A key translates symbols

On screen: Symbols simplify features. / The key explains their meanings.

A symbol stands for a feature so the map can be read without drawing every detail. A dot may mark a city, and a line may mark a road or river. Colours and shapes should be interpreted using the supplied key, not by assuming they always mean the same thing. Compare two possible keys for the same drawing. If a circle means a pond in one map and a town in another, the keys prevent confusion. Good map design keeps the meanings consistent within a map.

Brief check: Can we decide a symbol’s meaning from its colour alone?
Listen for: Use the key; colour alone may be ambiguous.

Check the date and scale

On screen: The date affects how current the map is. / The scale affects distance and detail.

A map may be excellent for one question and unsuitable for another. An old map can show past land use but may miss new roads. A small-scale regional map covers a broad area but may omit a local path. A large-scale map usually has more space for local detail. Date and scale therefore affect interpretation, alongside purpose. Demonstrate choosing a map for a local walking route and another for locating a country. The best map is the one whose information matches the geographical question.

Brief check: Which matters when checking a recently built road?
Listen for: The map’s date and whether it shows that level of detail.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Scale connects the map to the ground

On screen: 1 cm can represent many metres. / Keep map units and ground units separate.

A map shrinks a place so it fits on a page or screen. Scale tells us how much ground distance is represented by a drawing distance. If one centimetre represents twenty metres, the centimetre belongs to the map and the metres belong to the ground. Show one centimetre, then two, then three equal sections. Their represented ground distances increase proportionally. Scale is a relationship, not an extra number to add to the measurement. Without it, a ruler tells us only the length of the drawing.

Brief check: Does one centimetre always represent twenty metres?
Listen for: No. It depends on the map’s scale.

From map distance to real distance

On screen: Measure the map line. / Multiply by the distance per centimetre.

At one centimetre to twenty metres, a five-centimetre path represents one hundred metres. Count five equal twenty-metre sections, then write five times twenty. Keep metres in the final answer. This concrete method shows why multiplication works before using a formula. If the line has several sections, add their map lengths before converting or convert each consistently and then add. Be careful not to measure a straight-line gap when the question asks for a route around obstacles.

Brief check: At 1 cm = 20 m, what does 2 cm represent?
Listen for: 40 m.

From ground distance to map distance

On screen: Choose the scale first. / Divide the ground distance by the scale value.

We can reverse the calculation when making a map. If one centimetre represents twenty metres, a hundred-metre boundary must be drawn as five centimetres. We divide one hundred by twenty to find how many map sections are needed. The unit of the answer is centimetres on the drawing. Check it by multiplying back to the original ground distance. A useful scale must also allow the whole area to fit on the page. A correct conversion that extends beyond the page is unsuitable for that drawing task.

Brief check: How can we check a reverse calculation?
Listen for: Multiply the map length by the scale and recover the ground distance.

Resizing changes the displayed scale

On screen: Enlarging doubles drawing lengths. / The actual ground distance stays the same.

Imagine enlarging a map to twice its original width and height. The places have not moved farther apart on the ground, but every drawn line is twice as long. The same real distance is now represented by more centimetres, so metres per displayed centimetre are smaller. A scale bar enlarged together with the map preserves its visual relationship; a printed ratio or statement must be interpreted for the new size. This is why measuring a projected picture with an ordinary ruler can be misleading.

Brief check: Does enlarging a map make the real journey longer?
Listen for: No. It changes the drawing, not the ground distance.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Scale connects the map to the ground

On screen: 1 cm can represent many metres. / Keep map units and ground units separate.

A map shrinks a place so it fits on a page or screen. Scale tells us how much ground distance is represented by a drawing distance. If one centimetre represents twenty metres, the centimetre belongs to the map and the metres belong to the ground. Show one centimetre, then two, then three equal sections. Their represented ground distances increase proportionally. Scale is a relationship, not an extra number to add to the measurement. Without it, a ruler tells us only the length of the drawing.

Brief check: Does one centimetre always represent twenty metres?
Listen for: No. It depends on the map’s scale.

From map distance to real distance

On screen: Measure the map line. / Multiply by the distance per centimetre.

At one centimetre to twenty metres, a five-centimetre path represents one hundred metres. Count five equal twenty-metre sections, then write five times twenty. Keep metres in the final answer. This concrete method shows why multiplication works before using a formula. If the line has several sections, add their map lengths before converting or convert each consistently and then add. Be careful not to measure a straight-line gap when the question asks for a route around obstacles.

Brief check: At 1 cm = 20 m, what does 2 cm represent?
Listen for: 40 m.

From ground distance to map distance

On screen: Choose the scale first. / Divide the ground distance by the scale value.

We can reverse the calculation when making a map. If one centimetre represents twenty metres, a hundred-metre boundary must be drawn as five centimetres. We divide one hundred by twenty to find how many map sections are needed. The unit of the answer is centimetres on the drawing. Check it by multiplying back to the original ground distance. A useful scale must also allow the whole area to fit on the page. A correct conversion that extends beyond the page is unsuitable for that drawing task.

Brief check: How can we check a reverse calculation?
Listen for: Multiply the map length by the scale and recover the ground distance.

Resizing changes the displayed scale

On screen: Enlarging doubles drawing lengths. / The actual ground distance stays the same.

Imagine enlarging a map to twice its original width and height. The places have not moved farther apart on the ground, but every drawn line is twice as long. The same real distance is now represented by more centimetres, so metres per displayed centimetre are smaller. A scale bar enlarged together with the map preserves its visual relationship; a printed ratio or statement must be interpreted for the new size. This is why measuring a projected picture with an ordinary ruler can be misleading.

Brief check: Does enlarging a map make the real journey longer?
Listen for: No. It changes the drawing, not the ground distance.

Mental maps are selective

On screen: We remember routes and landmarks. / Different people remember different features.

A mental map is a person’s remembered view of a place. It often includes familiar routes, important landmarks and destinations, while omitting unfamiliar areas. Two pupils can know the same neighbourhood but remember different features because they travel differently or value different places. A mental map can be useful without being perfectly measured. Explain its purpose: showing remembered relationships. Do not call every omission a mistake. The important question is whether the remembered information is sufficient and accurate for the task we want to perform.

Brief check: Why might two people’s remembered maps differ?
Listen for: Their experiences, routes and priorities can differ.

Landmarks help us navigate

On screen: A landmark is recognisable. / It helps us locate a turn or destination.

A useful landmark is something a traveller can recognise at the right point. “Turn beside the bridge” may be clearer than “turn after a while”. Follow a route using named landmarks in order. Explain how a landmark helps distinguish one junction from another. However, a shop sign can change and a small feature may be hard to see at night. Familiarity affects usefulness: a landmark obvious to one person may mean nothing to a visitor. A clear route description names features that the intended traveller can identify.

Brief check: What makes “after a while” a weak direction?
Listen for: It gives no clear landmark or measurable point.

Keep the route order

On screen: Start → landmark → turn → destination. / A missing step can break the journey.

Show a sequence of familiar places and trace it from the start. The order matters: the same landmarks in a different order may describe a different route. Include the direction of a turn where needed. Describe the journey aloud while moving a finger, then deliberately omit a step. Explain why the traveller would not know what to do at that point. A mental map is a provisional aid; important routes should be checked against current maps or direct observation when mistakes could prevent reaching the destination.

Brief check: Does a list of landmarks always give a usable route?
Listen for: No. Their sequence and connections must be clear.

Check memory against evidence

On screen: Compare remembered and mapped locations. / Update information that has changed.

Memory can distort distance and direction. A familiar walk may feel short, while an unfamiliar one feels longer even if their measured distances are similar. Compare a remembered route with a suitable map and identify a difference. Check whether the memory is inaccurate or the map is outdated. New construction, closures and changed landmarks can make old directions unsuitable. Updating a mental map is therefore an evidence task. Keep reliable remembered features while correcting the specific relationships that the comparison shows are wrong.

Brief check: Does a route feeling short establish its measured distance?
Listen for: No. Use suitable distance evidence.

Words for today

On screen: Aerial view: A view from above. An overhead photograph of school grounds. / Key: An explanation of map symbols. The key tells us which symbol means school. / Plan: A view from directly above. Simplify the view while keeping positions.

Aerial view: A view from above. Example: An overhead photograph of school grounds. Key: An explanation of map symbols. Example: The key tells us which symbol means school.
