A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Aerial views look down

On screen: A photograph records visible detail. / A plan shows positions using simpler shapes.

An aerial view looks down towards the ground. It can reveal the arrangement of buildings, roads, vegetation and water more clearly than a view from street level. A photograph includes texture and shadows; a plan simplifies features into shapes and symbols. Point to one feature in the photograph and its matching position in the plan. We should preserve the important spatial relationships even when removing detail. A plan need not draw every roof tile to show where a building lies relative to a road.

Brief check: What should remain when detail is simplified?
Listen for: The relevant positions and spatial relationships.

Match features by their position

On screen: Use north, east, south and west. / Look for neighbouring features.

To translate an aerial view into a plan, identify a few stable features first. A pond west of a building should remain west of it in a north-up plan. Use neighbouring features as well as shape: a rectangular roof beside a playground can help identify a school. Camera angle and shadows may make appearances misleading, so avoid relying on one visual clue alone. Demonstrate matching the feature, locating it relative to others, and then replacing it with a simple symbol at the corresponding position.

Brief check: If north is up, where does a western feature belong?
Listen for: To the left of the reference feature.

Make a consistent key

On screen: One symbol has one meaning. / Use distinct symbols for different features.

A key is a translation between map symbols and real features. A blue circle for a pond and a rectangle for a building can work if their meanings are explained. If the plan uses the same symbol for different features without explanation, readers may confuse them. Show a deliberately mismatched key and correct either the symbol or the label so they agree. The task is consistency, not choosing one universally perfect symbol. Symbols should also be readable at the size in which the map will be used.

Brief check: What is wrong if the key says pond but the symbol marks a school?
Listen for: The symbol and key do not match.

Simplification has limits

On screen: A plan can show arrangement. / It may not show height or current use.

A simple plan can show where features are, but may not reveal how tall a building is or what happens inside it. An aerial photograph can show a roof without proving the building’s current purpose. Explain what each source directly provides and what needs another source. A simplified school plan may be excellent for finding the library but unsuitable for assessing a steep path unless height or slope information is included. Good geographical interpretation chooses the source that measures the property in the question.

Brief check: Does a roof shape prove what a building is used for today?
Listen for: No. Its use needs other evidence.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Scale connects the map to the ground

On screen: 1 cm can represent many metres. / Keep map units and ground units separate.

A map shrinks a place so it fits on a page or screen. Scale tells us how much ground distance is represented by a drawing distance. If one centimetre represents twenty metres, the centimetre belongs to the map and the metres belong to the ground. Show one centimetre, then two, then three equal sections. Their represented ground distances increase proportionally. Scale is a relationship, not an extra number to add to the measurement. Without it, a ruler tells us only the length of the drawing.

Brief check: Does one centimetre always represent twenty metres?
Listen for: No. It depends on the map’s scale.

Resizing changes the displayed scale

On screen: Enlarging doubles drawing lengths. / The actual ground distance stays the same.

Imagine enlarging a map to twice its original width and height. The places have not moved farther apart on the ground, but every drawn line is twice as long. The same real distance is now represented by more centimetres, so metres per displayed centimetre are smaller. A scale bar enlarged together with the map preserves its visual relationship; a printed ratio or statement must be interpreted for the new size. This is why measuring a projected picture with an ordinary ruler can be misleading.

Brief check: Does enlarging a map make the real journey longer?
Listen for: No. It changes the drawing, not the ground distance.

Mental maps are selective

On screen: We remember routes and landmarks. / Different people remember different features.

A mental map is a person’s remembered view of a place. It often includes familiar routes, important landmarks and destinations, while omitting unfamiliar areas. Two pupils can know the same neighbourhood but remember different features because they travel differently or value different places. A mental map can be useful without being perfectly measured. Explain its purpose: showing remembered relationships. Do not call every omission a mistake. The important question is whether the remembered information is sufficient and accurate for the task we want to perform.

Brief check: Why might two people’s remembered maps differ?
Listen for: Their experiences, routes and priorities can differ.

Check memory against evidence

On screen: Compare remembered and mapped locations. / Update information that has changed.

Memory can distort distance and direction. A familiar walk may feel short, while an unfamiliar one feels longer even if their measured distances are similar. Compare a remembered route with a suitable map and identify a difference. Check whether the memory is inaccurate or the map is outdated. New construction, closures and changed landmarks can make old directions unsuitable. Updating a mental map is therefore an evidence task. Keep reliable remembered features while correcting the specific relationships that the comparison shows are wrong.

Brief check: Does a route feeling short establish its measured distance?
Listen for: No. Use suitable distance evidence.

Aerial views look down

On screen: A photograph records visible detail. / A plan shows positions using simpler shapes.

An aerial view looks down towards the ground. It can reveal the arrangement of buildings, roads, vegetation and water more clearly than a view from street level. A photograph includes texture and shadows; a plan simplifies features into shapes and symbols. Point to one feature in the photograph and its matching position in the plan. We should preserve the important spatial relationships even when removing detail. A plan need not draw every roof tile to show where a building lies relative to a road.

Brief check: What should remain when detail is simplified?
Listen for: The relevant positions and spatial relationships.

Simplification has limits

On screen: A plan can show arrangement. / It may not show height or current use.

A simple plan can show where features are, but may not reveal how tall a building is or what happens inside it. An aerial photograph can show a roof without proving the building’s current purpose. Explain what each source directly provides and what needs another source. A simplified school plan may be excellent for finding the library but unsuitable for assessing a steep path unless height or slope information is included. Good geographical interpretation chooses the source that measures the property in the question.

Brief check: Does a roof shape prove what a building is used for today?
Listen for: No. Its use needs other evidence.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Aerial views look down

On screen: A photograph records visible detail. / A plan shows positions using simpler shapes.

An aerial view looks down towards the ground. It can reveal the arrangement of buildings, roads, vegetation and water more clearly than a view from street level. A photograph includes texture and shadows; a plan simplifies features into shapes and symbols. Point to one feature in the photograph and its matching position in the plan. We should preserve the important spatial relationships even when removing detail. A plan need not draw every roof tile to show where a building lies relative to a road.

Brief check: What should remain when detail is simplified?
Listen for: The relevant positions and spatial relationships.

Match features by their position

On screen: Use north, east, south and west. / Look for neighbouring features.

To translate an aerial view into a plan, identify a few stable features first. A pond west of a building should remain west of it in a north-up plan. Use neighbouring features as well as shape: a rectangular roof beside a playground can help identify a school. Camera angle and shadows may make appearances misleading, so avoid relying on one visual clue alone. Demonstrate matching the feature, locating it relative to others, and then replacing it with a simple symbol at the corresponding position.

Brief check: If north is up, where does a western feature belong?
Listen for: To the left of the reference feature.

Make a consistent key

On screen: One symbol has one meaning. / Use distinct symbols for different features.

A key is a translation between map symbols and real features. A blue circle for a pond and a rectangle for a building can work if their meanings are explained. If the plan uses the same symbol for different features without explanation, readers may confuse them. Show a deliberately mismatched key and correct either the symbol or the label so they agree. The task is consistency, not choosing one universally perfect symbol. Symbols should also be readable at the size in which the map will be used.

Brief check: What is wrong if the key says pond but the symbol marks a school?
Listen for: The symbol and key do not match.

Simplification has limits

On screen: A plan can show arrangement. / It may not show height or current use.

A simple plan can show where features are, but may not reveal how tall a building is or what happens inside it. An aerial photograph can show a roof without proving the building’s current purpose. Explain what each source directly provides and what needs another source. A simplified school plan may be excellent for finding the library but unsuitable for assessing a steep path unless height or slope information is included. Good geographical interpretation chooses the source that measures the property in the question.

Brief check: Does a roof shape prove what a building is used for today?
Listen for: No. Its use needs other evidence.

A grid gives a shared location system

On screen: Eastings go across. / Northings go up.

Grid lines provide a common way to locate places on a map. Easting numbers increase towards the east; northing numbers increase towards the north. Always read eastings first. Trace across the map before moving up and say the order aloud. A reference is meaningful within its map or grid system, so it should not be treated as an address that works everywhere. On Ordnance Survey maps, the National Grid also uses a letter prefix to identify the larger grid area. Our exercise uses a small practice grid.

Brief check: Which do we read first?
Listen for: Eastings first, then northings.

Four figures identify a square

On screen: Use the square’s left easting. / Then use its bottom northing.

A four-figure reference identifies a grid square, rather than one exact point. Locate the left boundary of the square and read its easting. Locate the bottom boundary and read its northing. Join these two two-digit values in that order. For practice square 2345, twenty-three is the left easting and forty-five the bottom northing. Do not use the nearest line without checking which boundary it represents. Several features can share the same four-figure square, which explains why more detail may be needed.

Brief check: Does 2345 identify just one building?
Listen for: No. It identifies a square that may contain several features.

Six figures add tenths

On screen: Divide the square into ten parts across. / Then divide it into ten parts up.

To locate a point more precisely, estimate tenths within the square. Add the across tenth to the easting half, then add the upward tenth to the northing half. In square 2345, a point six tenths across and two tenths up becomes 236452. Build the two halves separately: two-three-six, then four-five-two. This reduces the risk of putting both tenths at the end. On a one-kilometre National Grid square, a six-figure reference identifies a one-hundred-metre square rather than a perfectly exact mathematical point.

Brief check: What changes when only the easting tenth increases?
Listen for: The location moves east within the practice square.

Check by plotting back

On screen: Read the two halves separately. / Plot the result and compare with the target.

A reference should lead another reader back to the intended location. Split the six figures into easting and northing halves, identify the square, then position the tenths. If the point appears in the wrong part of the square, check whether the tenths were swapped or the order reversed. Show the original target beside a wrongly plotted point. A valid-looking string of six digits is not enough: it must match the intended place. Plotting back checks the meaning of the answer rather than just its format.

Brief check: Why is plotting back useful?
Listen for: It tests whether the reference actually identifies the intended location.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Easting: A numbered line read across the map. Read across to easting 23. / Northing: A numbered line read up the map. Read up to northing 45. / Grid reference: Numbers locating a square or point. Square 2345; add tenths for a precise point.

Easting: A numbered line read across the map. Example: Read across to easting 23. Northing: A numbered line read up the map. Example: Read up to northing 45. Grid reference: Numbers locating a square or point. Example: Square 2345; add tenths for a precise point. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

A grid gives a shared location system

On screen: Eastings go across. / Northings go up.

Grid lines provide a common way to locate places on a map. Easting numbers increase towards the east; northing numbers increase towards the north. Always read eastings first. Trace across the map before moving up and say the order aloud. A reference is meaningful within its map or grid system, so it should not be treated as an address that works everywhere. On Ordnance Survey maps, the National Grid also uses a letter prefix to identify the larger grid area. Our exercise uses a small practice grid.

Brief check: Which do we read first?
Listen for: Eastings first, then northings.

Four figures identify a square

On screen: Use the square’s left easting. / Then use its bottom northing.

A four-figure reference identifies a grid square, rather than one exact point. Locate the left boundary of the square and read its easting. Locate the bottom boundary and read its northing. Join these two two-digit values in that order. For practice square 2345, twenty-three is the left easting and forty-five the bottom northing. Do not use the nearest line without checking which boundary it represents. Several features can share the same four-figure square, which explains why more detail may be needed.

Brief check: Does 2345 identify just one building?
Listen for: No. It identifies a square that may contain several features.

Six figures add tenths

On screen: Divide the square into ten parts across. / Then divide it into ten parts up.

To locate a point more precisely, estimate tenths within the square. Add the across tenth to the easting half, then add the upward tenth to the northing half. In square 2345, a point six tenths across and two tenths up becomes 236452. Build the two halves separately: two-three-six, then four-five-two. This reduces the risk of putting both tenths at the end. On a one-kilometre National Grid square, a six-figure reference identifies a one-hundred-metre square rather than a perfectly exact mathematical point.

Brief check: What changes when only the easting tenth increases?
Listen for: The location moves east within the practice square.

Check by plotting back

On screen: Read the two halves separately. / Plot the result and compare with the target.

A reference should lead another reader back to the intended location. Split the six figures into easting and northing halves, identify the square, then position the tenths. If the point appears in the wrong part of the square, check whether the tenths were swapped or the order reversed. Show the original target beside a wrongly plotted point. A valid-looking string of six digits is not enough: it must match the intended place. Plotting back checks the meaning of the answer rather than just its format.

Brief check: Why is plotting back useful?
Listen for: It tests whether the reference actually identifies the intended location.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Scale: The link between map and real distance. At 1 cm = 100 m, 4 cm represents 400 m. / Distance: How far apart places are. Add every section of the walking route. / Unit: A measurement such as metres. 400 m, not an unexplained “400”.

Scale: The link between map and real distance. Example: At 1 cm = 100 m, 4 cm represents 400 m. Distance: How far apart places are. Example: Add every section of the walking route. Unit: A measurement such as metres. Example: 400 m, not an unexplained “400”. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Direct distance and route distance

On screen: Direct distance joins start and finish. / Route distance follows the usable path.

Direct distance is the straight-line separation between two places. Route distance follows the actual journey, including bends and detours. A river or fence can make the route longer than the direct line. Show both on the same drawing and trace each separately. Before measuring, decide which distance the question asks for. The shortest visible line is not automatically a usable route. Geography uses distance alongside connections and barriers to explain why places that look close together can take longer to reach.

Brief check: Which distance includes the detour around a fence?
Listen for: Route distance.

Add all route sections

On screen: Measure each section once. / Use the same unit throughout.

A route made of several straight sections can be measured section by section. Label each length so no section is missed or counted twice. Add map lengths in the same unit before converting with the scale. If the route has two, three and one centimetre sections, its map length is six centimetres. Explain why we do not include the direct gap as another section. It is a different measurement of the same start and destination. Keep the route visibly highlighted while building the addition.

Brief check: Do we add the direct gap to the route sections?
Listen for: No. The direct gap is not an extra travelled section.

Use scale to compare fairly

On screen: Convert both routes with their map scales. / Compare ground distances in the same unit.

A drawn line is not a real distance until we apply its map scale. Two routes on the same map can be compared using the same metres-per-centimetre relationship. If they are on different maps, their scales may differ, so compare their converted ground distances rather than drawing lengths. Change metres to kilometres consistently when necessary. A shorter drawn route can represent a longer real route if its map covers much more ground per centimetre. The scale is part of the evidence, not a detail to ignore.

Brief check: Can we compare centimetres from two different scales directly?
Listen for: No. Convert to comparable ground distances first.

Distance is one part of a recommendation

On screen: Check access and closures. / Then compare time or convenience.

A route recommendation needs the traveller’s needs and current conditions as well as distance. A shorter route may include stairs or a closed crossing. A longer one may be the only feasible route. Explain the sequence: confirm the route connects the required places, check that it can be used, then compare distance or other preferences. Do not assume a map shows today’s service status. A careful recommendation states the condition on which it depends and names one relevant check before a real journey.

Brief check: What could make the shorter route unsuitable?
Listen for: A barrier, closure or access problem for the traveller.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Direct distance and route distance

On screen: Direct distance joins start and finish. / Route distance follows the usable path.

Direct distance is the straight-line separation between two places. Route distance follows the actual journey, including bends and detours. A river or fence can make the route longer than the direct line. Show both on the same drawing and trace each separately. Before measuring, decide which distance the question asks for. The shortest visible line is not automatically a usable route. Geography uses distance alongside connections and barriers to explain why places that look close together can take longer to reach.

Brief check: Which distance includes the detour around a fence?
Listen for: Route distance.

Add all route sections

On screen: Measure each section once. / Use the same unit throughout.

A route made of several straight sections can be measured section by section. Label each length so no section is missed or counted twice. Add map lengths in the same unit before converting with the scale. If the route has two, three and one centimetre sections, its map length is six centimetres. Explain why we do not include the direct gap as another section. It is a different measurement of the same start and destination. Keep the route visibly highlighted while building the addition.

Brief check: Do we add the direct gap to the route sections?
Listen for: No. The direct gap is not an extra travelled section.

Use scale to compare fairly

On screen: Convert both routes with their map scales. / Compare ground distances in the same unit.

A drawn line is not a real distance until we apply its map scale. Two routes on the same map can be compared using the same metres-per-centimetre relationship. If they are on different maps, their scales may differ, so compare their converted ground distances rather than drawing lengths. Change metres to kilometres consistently when necessary. Brief check: Can we compare centimetres from two different scales directly?
Listen for: No. Convert to comparable ground distances first.

Distance is one part of a recommendation

On screen: Check access and closures. / Then compare time or convenience.

A route recommendation needs the traveller’s needs and current conditions as well as distance. A shorter route may include stairs or a closed crossing. A longer one may be the only feasible route. Explain the sequence: confirm the route connects the required places, check that it can be used, then compare distance or other preferences. Do not assume a map shows today’s service status. A careful recommendation states the condition on which it depends and names one relevant check before a real journey.

Brief check: What could make the shorter route unsuitable?
Listen for: A barrier, closure or access problem for the traveller.

Read an OS map’s information

On screen: Read the legend and symbols. / Check scale and grid information.

Ordnance Survey maps use symbols, a National Grid and scales to describe places in Great Britain. Begin with the map information rather than guessing from an isolated symbol. The legend explains the features shown, and the grid supports location references. A map designed for walking needs different detail from a broad regional map. Our classroom diagrams practise the skills but are not reproduced official map extracts. Explain that a real map’s edition and current conditions also matter when planning an outdoor route.

Brief check: What should we consult to decode an unfamiliar symbol?
Listen for: The map’s legend or key.

A ratio scale uses the same units

On screen: 1:25,000 means 1 unit to 25,000 units. / 1 cm represents 250 m.

A ratio scale compares like units. At one to twenty-five thousand, one centimetre on the map represents twenty-five thousand centimetres on the ground. Convert those ground centimetres to metres by dividing by one hundred: the result is two hundred and fifty metres. Write the conversion as a sequence rather than skipping the units. A pupil who reports twenty-five thousand metres has retained the number but changed the unit incorrectly. The ratio itself does not require centimetres, but both sides must use the same unit before conversion.

Brief check: Why is 25,000 cm not 25,000 m?
Listen for: A metre contains one hundred centimetres.

Coverage and detail change with scale

On screen: 1:25,000 usually shows more local detail. / 1:250,000 covers more ground in the same space.

At one to two hundred and fifty thousand, each map centimetre represents two thousand five hundred metres. That is ten times the ground distance represented at one to twenty-five thousand. The broader-scale map fits more territory on a page but has less room for small features. The smaller denominator is called the larger scale. Explain the relationship with the ground distance rather than expecting pupils to memorise the terminology alone. Choose a scale according to whether we need local walking detail or a broad overview.

Brief check: Which gives more page space to one kilometre?
Listen for: The 1:25,000 map.

Symbols do not guarantee access

On screen: An intersection may need a crossing. / Current access needs a separate check.

A footpath line crossing a stream line raises a practical question: how does the traveller cross? Look for the relevant crossing information, but do not assume that every intersection is a safe bridge. Map symbols provide evidence about selected features at the map’s date; they do not guarantee present safety or permission. Conditions can change after publication. Model a route decision that uses scale, symbols and a clearly stated check. This joins map reading to sensible interpretation without turning a classroom drawing into live travel advice.

Brief check: Does two crossing lines automatically mean a safe bridge?
Listen for: No. Check the crossing information and current conditions.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Read an OS map’s information

On screen: Read the legend and symbols. / Check scale and grid information.

Ordnance Survey maps use symbols, a National Grid and scales to describe places in Great Britain. Begin with the map information rather than guessing from an isolated symbol. The legend explains the features shown, and the grid supports location references. A map designed for walking needs different detail from a broad regional map. Our classroom diagrams practise the skills but are not reproduced official map extracts. Explain that a real map’s edition and current conditions also matter when planning an outdoor route.

Brief check: What should we consult to decode an unfamiliar symbol?
Listen for: The map’s legend or key.

A ratio scale uses the same units

On screen: 1:25,000 means 1 unit to 25,000 units. / 1 cm represents 250 m.

A ratio scale compares like units. At one to twenty-five thousand, one centimetre on the map represents twenty-five thousand centimetres on the ground. Convert those ground centimetres to metres by dividing by one hundred: the result is two hundred and fifty metres. Write the conversion as a sequence rather than skipping the units. A pupil who reports twenty-five thousand metres has retained the number but changed the unit incorrectly. The ratio itself does not require centimetres, but both sides must use the same unit before conversion.

Brief check: Why is 25,000 cm not 25,000 m?
Listen for: A metre contains one hundred centimetres.

Coverage and detail change with scale

On screen: 1:25,000 usually shows more local detail. / 1:250,000 covers more ground in the same space.

At one to two hundred and fifty thousand, each map centimetre represents two thousand five hundred metres. That is ten times the ground distance represented at one to twenty-five thousand. The broader-scale map fits more territory on a page but has less room for small features. The smaller denominator is called the larger scale. Explain the relationship with the ground distance rather than expecting pupils to memorise the terminology alone. Choose a scale according to whether we need local walking detail or a broad overview.

Brief check: Which gives more page space to one kilometre?
Listen for: The 1:25,000 map.

Symbols do not guarantee access

On screen: An intersection may need a crossing. / Current access needs a separate check.

A footpath line crossing a stream line raises a practical question: how does the traveller cross? Look for the relevant crossing information, but do not assume that every intersection is a safe bridge. Map symbols provide evidence about selected features at the map’s date; they do not guarantee present safety or permission. Conditions can change after publication. Model a route decision that uses scale, symbols and a clearly stated check. This joins map reading to sensible interpretation without turning a classroom drawing into live travel advice.

Brief check: Does two crossing lines automatically mean a safe bridge?
Listen for: No. Check the crossing information and current conditions.

Height and steepness differ

On screen: Height is a level above a reference. / Steepness compares rise with horizontal distance.

A summit can be high but reached by a gentle slope. A lower hill can have a steep side. Height describes a level, usually relative to a reference such as mean sea level. Steepness describes how quickly height changes over horizontal distance. Demonstrate two paths with the same rise but different horizontal lengths. The shorter horizontal path is steeper on average. Separating these ideas prevents us from calling the highest part of every profile the steepest simply because it is at the top.

Brief check: Is the highest point always on the steepest slope?
Listen for: No. Height and rate of height change are different.

Contours join equal heights

On screen: Each contour represents one height. / Read the contour interval.

A contour line joins points of equal height. The contour interval is the vertical difference between neighbouring contour levels. Find the interval before judging slope or counting levels. On a map with a fixed interval, closely spaced contours show a large height change across a short horizontal distance. Widely spaced ones show a gentler slope. Compare spacing within the same map first. Between different maps, interval and scale may differ, so spacing alone does not give a fair comparison of real steepness.

Brief check: What extra information matters when comparing different contour maps?
Listen for: Their contour intervals and horizontal scales.

A profile shows a side view

On screen: Horizontal axis: distance. / Vertical axis: height.

A profile turns height information along a chosen line into a side view. Mark the distance positions along the horizontal axis, then plot the corresponding heights on the vertical axis. Join the points to show the sampled shape. Both axes need labels and scales. The appearance of steepness can change if we exaggerate the vertical scale, so it is important to state how the drawing was made. A profile describes one selected line through the landscape; it does not show every direction across the whole hill.

Brief check: Which axis shows height?
Listen for: The vertical axis.

Compare rise over run

On screen: Rise = ending height − starting height. / Use the same horizontal distance for a direct comparison.

For equal horizontal intervals, the greatest rise identifies the steepest average interval. If the distances differ, compare both rise and run rather than the rise alone. A forty-metre rise over one hundred metres is steeper than the same rise over two hundred metres. Show the two right-angle triangles and describe the difference before calculating. Average slope summarises the interval and can hide smaller changes within it. Explain which section the conclusion refers to so pupils do not extend one result to the whole route.

Brief check: Which is steeper: the same rise over 100 m or 200 m?
Listen for: Over 100 m, because the height changes over a shorter horizontal distance.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Latitude: Position north or south of the Equator. 20°N is north of the Equator. / Longitude: Position east or west of the prime meridian. 30°W is west of the prime meridian. / Equator: The line at zero degrees latitude. 0° latitude separates north from south.

Latitude: Position north or south of the Equator. Example: 20°N is north of the Equator. Longitude: Position east or west of the prime meridian. Example: 30°W is west of the prime meridian. Equator: The line at zero degrees latitude. Example: 0° latitude separates north from south. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Latitude measures north or south

On screen: The Equator is 0° latitude. / Use N or S for non-zero latitude.

Latitude describes a position north or south of the Equator using an angle measured in degrees. The Equator is zero degrees latitude. Trace it around the globe, then point to a place north and a place south. Lines of latitude run around the globe, but the value tells us north-south position. This distinction can confuse learners: the direction of the line is not the direction represented by its value. Latitude alone does not identify one place because many places share the same latitude.

Brief check: Does 20°N identify one unique place?
Listen for: No. Many places share that latitude.

Longitude measures east or west

On screen: The prime meridian is 0° longitude. / Use E or W for non-zero longitude.

Longitude describes east-west position relative to the prime meridian. Meridians run between the poles, but the longitude value tells us how far east or west the location lies in angular terms. Point to the zero line, then compare a location east of it with one west of it. Do not confuse the letter E in longitude with a local journey direction: a point can have an eastern longitude and still travel west to another place. Coordinates describe locations within a global reference system.

Brief check: What does W mean in a longitude?
Listen for: West of the prime meridian.

Use both coordinates

On screen: Latitude first, longitude second. / Keep degrees and direction letters together.

A full coordinate pair joins north-south and east-west information. Twenty degrees north and thirty degrees east identifies the intersection of two reference lines. Build the answer in two parts and retain the direction letters. Twenty north, thirty west is a different place from twenty north, thirty east. At zero latitude the point is on the Equator; a north or south label is not needed to distinguish a hemisphere. Ask pupils to follow each line to the intersection rather than treating the pair as unrelated numbers.

Brief check: What changes if E is replaced by W?
Listen for: The point moves to the other side of the prime meridian at that longitude value.

Degrees are angles, not kilometres

On screen: Coordinate differences describe angular position. / Ground distance needs more information.

A difference of ten degrees is not automatically a fixed number of kilometres in every direction and location. In particular, meridians become closer towards the poles, so a degree of longitude represents different ground distances at different latitudes. Our introductory task locates places rather than calculating those distances. Emphasise the units: degrees for coordinates, metres or kilometres for ground length. Use this distinction to check an answer that labels a longitude difference in kilometres without a suitable calculation or location information.

Brief check: Can we simply replace degrees with kilometres?
Listen for: No. They are different quantities.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Read an OS map’s information

On screen: Read the legend and symbols. / Check scale and grid information.

Ordnance Survey maps use symbols, a National Grid and scales to describe places in Great Britain. Begin with the map information rather than guessing from an isolated symbol. The legend explains the features shown, and the grid supports location references. A map designed for walking needs different detail from a broad regional map. Our classroom diagrams practise the skills but are not reproduced official map extracts. Explain that a real map’s edition and current conditions also matter when planning an outdoor route.

Brief check: What should we consult to decode an unfamiliar symbol?
Listen for: The map’s legend or key.

Symbols do not guarantee access

On screen: An intersection may need a crossing. / Current access needs a separate check.

A footpath line crossing a stream line raises a practical question: how does the traveller cross? Look for the relevant crossing information, but do not assume that every intersection is a safe bridge. Map symbols provide evidence about selected features at the map’s date; they do not guarantee present safety or permission. Conditions can change after publication. Model a route decision that uses scale, symbols and a clearly stated check. This joins map reading to sensible interpretation without turning a classroom drawing into live travel advice.

Brief check: Does two crossing lines automatically mean a safe bridge?
Listen for: No. Check the crossing information and current conditions.

Height and steepness differ

On screen: Height is a level above a reference. / Steepness compares rise with horizontal distance.

A summit can be high but reached by a gentle slope. A lower hill can have a steep side. Height describes a level, usually relative to a reference such as mean sea level. Steepness describes how quickly height changes over horizontal distance. Demonstrate two paths with the same rise but different horizontal lengths. The shorter horizontal path is steeper on average. Separating these ideas prevents us from calling the highest part of every profile the steepest simply because it is at the top.

Brief check: Is the highest point always on the steepest slope?
Listen for: No. Height and rate of height change are different.

Compare rise over run

On screen: Rise = ending height − starting height. / Use the same horizontal distance for a direct comparison.

For equal horizontal intervals, the greatest rise identifies the steepest average interval. If the distances differ, compare both rise and run rather than the rise alone. A forty-metre rise over one hundred metres is steeper than the same rise over two hundred metres. Show the two right-angle triangles and describe the difference before calculating. Average slope summarises the interval and can hide smaller changes within it. Explain which section the conclusion refers to so pupils do not extend one result to the whole route.

Brief check: Which is steeper: the same rise over 100 m or 200 m?
Listen for: Over 100 m, because the height changes over a shorter horizontal distance.

Latitude measures north or south

On screen: The Equator is 0° latitude. / Use N or S for non-zero latitude.

Latitude describes a position north or south of the Equator using an angle measured in degrees. The Equator is zero degrees latitude. Trace it around the globe, then point to a place north and a place south. Lines of latitude run around the globe, but the value tells us north-south position. This distinction can confuse learners: the direction of the line is not the direction represented by its value. Latitude alone does not identify one place because many places share the same latitude.

Brief check: Does 20°N identify one unique place?
Listen for: No. Many places share that latitude.

Degrees are angles, not kilometres

On screen: Coordinate differences describe angular position. / Ground distance needs more information.

A difference of ten degrees is not automatically a fixed number of kilometres in every direction and location. In particular, meridians become closer towards the poles, so a degree of longitude represents different ground distances at different latitudes. Our introductory task locates places rather than calculating those distances. Emphasise the units: degrees for coordinates, metres or kilometres for ground length. Use this distinction to check an answer that labels a longitude difference in kilometres without a suitable calculation or location information.

Brief check: Can we simply replace degrees with kilometres?
Listen for: No. They are different quantities.

Latitude alone does not identify one place because many places share the same latitude.

Brief check: Does 20°N identify one unique place?
Listen for: No. Many places share that latitude.

Degrees are angles, not kilometres

On screen: Coordinate differences describe angular position. / Ground distance needs more information.

A difference of ten degrees is not automatically a fixed number of kilometres in every direction and location. In particular, meridians become closer towards the poles, so a degree of longitude represents different ground distances at different latitudes. Our introductory task locates places rather than calculating those distances. Emphasise the units: degrees for coordinates, metres or kilometres for ground length. Use this distinction to check an answer that labels a longitude difference in kilometres without a suitable calculation or location information.

Brief check: Can we simply replace degrees with kilometres?
Listen for: No. They are different quantities.

7B · Week 1 · Lesson 2 · sections 3.1, 3.3

40-minute route: recall 4, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 8, worked example 5, practice 10, check 5, exit 3. Divide each section between the topics in combined lessons. Timings are estimates.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

Look at the map

On screen: Does every country boundary have sea on both sides?

Give pupils quiet thinking time. Ask them to find a boundary between two countries on the map. England and Wales, or England and Scotland, share a land boundary: there is no sea between them. Invite a short answer after pupils have thought.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can explain the difference between the UK and Great Britain.

On screen: The UK includes Northern Ireland. / Great Britain is an island. / Name the four countries of the UK. / Identify the three countries on Great Britain. / Show a shared land boundary.

Read the learning goal. Play the short map explanation: four countries belong to the UK; three are on Great Britain; Northern Ireland belongs to the UK but is on the island of Ireland. Pause or replay as needed. Point to England and Wales to connect the goal to the starter. The UK is a country made up of four constituent countries; Great Britain names an island.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: United Kingdom: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. / Great Britain: The island containing England, Scotland and Wales. / Island: Land surrounded by water on every side.

Read each English word and model its pronunciation. Use the smaller Chinese and Russian translations as support. Compare the two highlighted maps: Northern Ireland is included in the UK, but not in Great Britain. The island picture shows water all the way around the land.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

An island and a country are different

On screen: Island: land surrounded by water. / Country: a political area.

An island is a physical area of land surrounded by water. A country is a political area. These definitions answer different questions. One island can contain more than one country, and one political state can include territory on more than one island. Use the actual map outlines to establish this before introducing the group names. Point to the water around the land, then point to the internal country boundaries. A boundary line does not necessarily mean water separates the places on either side.

Brief check: Does every country boundary have sea on both sides?
Listen for: No. Countries can share land boundaries.

Water changes transport connections

On screen: Roads connect places on land. / A sea crossing needs a boat or aircraft.

Trace a journey from Wales to Northern Ireland. The locations explain why a continuous road route alone cannot cross the intervening sea. A ferry or flight provides the crossing, while coaches connect the start and destination to terminals. Each transfer creates another journey leg and may include waiting. Ports and airports are connection points, not the final destination by definition. The map establishes where places and water lie; a timetable establishes which service operates and when. We need both kinds of information to plan an actual connected journey.

Brief check: Why does a map not prove that a ferry runs today?
Listen for: Location information does not confirm a current service.

Weather and climate use different time scales

On screen: Weather: conditions at a time and place. / Climate: long-term patterns of weather.

Weather describes conditions such as temperature, rainfall and wind at a particular time and place. Climate describes their long-term patterns and variation. A rainy afternoon is weather; it does not by itself establish a place’s typical rainfall. Show two station readings and state their dates before comparing them. Then explain why many observations across years are needed to investigate climate. Avoid saying that weather is random or that climate never changes. They concern related atmospheric conditions examined over different time scales.

Brief check: Does one cold day prove a cold climate?
Listen for: No. Climate needs long-term observations.

The leeward side may be drier

On screen: Leeward is away from the incoming wind. / Descending air warms; a rain shadow may form.

After crossing the high ground, air can descend on the leeward side. Descending air warms, which can reduce relative humidity and discourage cloud formation. This helps explain a rain-shadow pattern. It does not mean that the leeward side can never receive rain: other weather systems and conditions also matter. Reverse the wind arrow and reconsider which side is windward. In the UK, western uplands often enhance rainfall from moist westerly air, but a simplified diagram does not predict every day’s weather at every station.

Brief check: If the wind reverses, must the windward side stay the same?
Listen for: No. It is defined by the incoming wind direction.

17–22 min · Worked example

Belfast is in the UK. Is it also on Great Britain?

On screen: Look at the map. Think quietly, then explain your answer.

Read the question without revealing the answer. Model finding Belfast in Northern Ireland, tracing the coastline of the island of Ireland, then comparing it with Great Britain. Invite pupils to answer with a reason from the map. Reveal: Belfast is in the UK, but on the island of Ireland, not Great Britain. Country membership and island location answer different questions.

Brief check: Why can Belfast be in the UK without being on Great Britain?
Listen for: The UK includes Northern Ireland, which is on the island of Ireland.

Less moisture arrives. What happens to rain?

On screen: Keep the wind and mountain the same.

Briefly recall the Stage 4 diagram rather than repeating the full explanation. Keep wind direction, mountain and other conditions the same; reduce only the incoming moisture. Trace the rising air and explain that it still cools, but there is less moisture available for precipitation. Ask for a prediction before revealing. Expect less rainfall, not a guarantee of no rain. A mountain does not create the missing water.

Brief check: Does the mountain create water when the incoming air has less moisture?
Listen for: No. Less moisture is available, so we expect less rainfall with other conditions unchanged.

Class board challenge · Locate the UK at island and country scales

On screen: Watch your teacher demonstrate one move. / One volunteer can come to the board; everyone else watches.

Introduce the rule before making a move. Great Britain is the island containing England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland is on the island of Ireland and is also part of the UK. Start with the islands, then add country names and surrounding waters. Explain why one choice fits and why the other does not. Political membership and island location are different kinds of information. Then invite a volunteer for one turn if useful. Take one brief response from the class and finish by restating the geographical idea. This is the one core board activity for this topic; the teacher may operate it throughout.

Class board challenge · Explain relief rainfall as a connected process

On screen: Watch your teacher demonstrate one move. / One volunteer can come to the board; everyone else watches.

Introduce the rule before making a move. Moist air rises over high ground and cools. Condensation can form cloud and precipitation. Descending air on the other side may be drier; wind and moisture supply matter, so a mountain does not guarantee rain every day. Explain why one choice fits and why the other does not. Cooling changes conditions for condensation; it does not create water. Then invite a volunteer for one turn if useful. Take one brief response from the class and finish by restating the geographical idea. This is the one core board activity for this topic; the teacher may operate it throughout.

Partners compare their work with the evidence, not just each other’s answers. Check Compare measurements from the same period. Link rising moist air, cooling and condensation. Distinguish a day’s weather from long-term climate. In combined lessons, each partner chooses a different investigation. Keep the original response and explain one revision.

Invite two short explanations, preferably different methods or conclusions. Check each against its case source. Expected reasoning for the final case: Correction: Less moisture is available for precipitation. Cooling changes conditions for condensation; it does not create water. A complete response must explain the method, not simply copy the correct choice. For a changed case, accept different answers only when the new condition actually supports them.

32–37 min · Check understanding

On screen: Find Cardiff. Name its country and its island. / Explain why the country name and island name are different.

Allow independent thinking without choices or finger voting. Ask two pupils to explain where Cardiff is and why the two place names describe different things. Listen for Wales as the country and Great Britain as the island. Ask pupils to point to the boundary and trace the coastline as evidence. Reveal the example only after their explanations. Accept equivalent wording; help pupils distinguish country boundaries from the sea around an island.

Explain how the mountain helps rain form

On screen: Follow the moist air from the sea up the mountain. / Explain the chain: rises → cools → condenses → rain can fall.

Ask pupils to explain the process in their own words rather than vote on choices. The arrow chain is a scaffold, not a complete answer: listen for causal links between rising, cooling, condensation and precipitation. Ask where the water came from. Invite two explanations before revealing the example. Correct the idea that the mountain creates water. Rain is possible under suitable conditions, not guaranteed whenever air rises.

Collect independent answers: Cardiff is in Wales, on the island of Great Britain. A country and an island describe different things.

On screen: Independently: explain how moist air rising over a mountain can lead to rainfall.

United Kingdom: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Example: Northern Ireland is included in the UK. Great Britain: The island of England, Scotland and Wales. Example: England, Scotland and Wales share this island. Island: Land surrounded by water. Example: Trace a coastline all the way around. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

An island and a country are different

On screen: Island: land surrounded by water. / Country: a political area.

An island is a physical area of land surrounded by water. A country is a political area. These definitions answer different questions. One island can contain more than one country, and one political state can include territory on more than one island. Use the actual map outlines to establish this before introducing the group names. Point to the water around the land, then point to the internal country boundaries. A boundary line does not necessarily mean water separates the places on either side.

Brief check: Does every country boundary have sea on both sides?
Listen for: No. Countries can share land boundaries.

United Kingdom and Great Britain

On screen: UK: England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland. / Great Britain: England, Scotland and Wales.

The United Kingdom includes England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Great Britain is the island containing England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland lies on the island of Ireland, which also contains the separate country Ireland. Trace the two islands first, then identify the four UK countries. Great Britain and the UK therefore name different groups. Belfast is in Northern Ireland and the UK, but not on Great Britain. Repeat that contrast while pointing to the map so pupils connect the language to the actual location.

Brief check: Which UK country is on a different island from England?
Listen for: Northern Ireland.

Locate the UK at two scales

On screen: The UK is off north-west mainland Europe. / Wales is west of England; Scotland is north.

A broad map locates the UK relative to mainland Europe. A closer map shows the countries and nearby seas. The North Sea lies east of Great Britain, the Atlantic Ocean to the west, and the English Channel between southern England and northern France. The Irish Sea lies between Great Britain and the island of Ireland. Use the north arrow before making directional statements. Then give a location at two scales: the UK off north-west Europe, and Wales west of England. Neither statement replaces the other; each answers a different location question.

Brief check: Which sea lies between the two islands?
Listen for: The Irish Sea.

Water changes transport connections

On screen: Roads connect places on land. / A sea crossing needs a boat or aircraft.

Trace a journey from Wales to Northern Ireland. The locations explain why a continuous road route alone cannot cross the intervening sea. A ferry or flight provides the crossing, while coaches connect the start and destination to terminals. Each transfer creates another journey leg and may include waiting. Ports and airports are connection points, not the final destination by definition. The map establishes where places and water lie; a timetable establishes which service operates and when. We need both kinds of information to plan an actual connected journey.

Brief check: Why does a map not prove that a ferry runs today?
Listen for: Location information does not confirm a current service.

Connect the journey legs

On screen: A route is a sequence of connected legs. / Start and destination tell us where; connections tell us how to get there.

A route is a sequence of connected legs. Start and destination tell us where; connections tell us how to get there. Crossing the Irish Sea requires a sea or air leg in this model.

Count travel and waiting

On screen: Total journey time includes waiting and transfers. / Worked example: a 1-hour bus, 2-hour wait and 2-hour crossing take 5 hours, not 3.

Total journey time includes waiting and transfers. Worked example: a 1-hour bus, 2-hour wait and 2-hour crossing take 5 hours, not 3. List every leg before adding.

Check the constraints

On screen: A constraint is a limit that must be satisfied. / If a journey costs 50 tokens and the budget is 40, being fast does not make it affordable.

A constraint is a limit that must be satisfied. If a journey costs 50 tokens and the budget is 40, being fast does not make it affordable. Compare feasibility first, then preferences.

Revise the decision

On screen: When a service is cancelled, update the plan rather than defend the old answer. / “None of these options currently works” can be the correct conclusion.

When a service is cancelled, update the plan rather than defend the old answer. “None of these options currently works” can be the correct conclusion. State what information or change would make travel possible.

A journey with 1 hour on a coach, 2 hours waiting and 2 hours crossing takes 5 hours. Count every leg, then check budget and availability. The fastest option is useless if it exceeds a fixed budget or is cancelled.

Feasibility requires satisfying the budget before comparing speed.

Contrast this with: The 5-hour trip because it is faster. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information. Then ask the class to explain one step in their own words.

Listen for: The 7-hour trip. Feasibility requires satisfying the budget before comparing speed.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Boundary: A line separating areas. England and Wales share a land boundary. / Region: An area with shared features. The Highlands are an upland region. / Physical feature: A natural part of the landscape. A river is a natural feature.

Boundary: A line separating areas. Example: England and Wales share a land boundary. Region: An area with shared features. Example: The Highlands are an upland region. Physical feature: A natural part of the landscape. Example: A river is a natural feature. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Political maps show territories

On screen: Countries and boundaries are political information. / Read what each colour represents.

A political map shows divisions such as countries and their boundaries. Colours make neighbouring territories easier to distinguish; they do not automatically represent temperature or height. Point to Wales and England and identify the line separating them. A country can contain rivers, cities and mountains, but its outline is not the shape of one landform. Begin with the legend to understand the layer we are reading. Different maps of the same area may use different colours while describing the same political division.

Brief check: Does a green country automatically mean low land?
Listen for: No. Its colour may simply identify the country.

Physical maps show land and water

On screen: Relief describes the shape and height of land. / Rivers and mountains are physical features.

A physical map focuses on natural features such as land height, mountains and rivers. Relief means the shape and height differences of the land. The Scottish Highlands are an upland region in northern Great Britain; they are not another country. Compare the Highlands label with the Scotland boundary so the two kinds of information remain distinct. Rivers can cross territorial boundaries because water follows the landscape rather than stopping at a political line. The key tells us whether shading represents height, land cover or another physical property.

Brief check: Is a mountain region the same thing as a country?
Listen for: No. They describe different kinds of area.

Combine layers for a better question

On screen: Country layer: where is the territory? / Relief layer: what is the land like?

Layers allow us to examine different information about the same place. A country layer locates Wales, while a relief layer helps us examine high and low ground. A river layer adds drainage information. Switch layers without changing the location, then explain what each contributes. A question about a route across high land may need more than a country boundary. However, adding many layers at once can make a map harder to read. Select the layers that help answer the geographical question rather than treating more information as automatically better.

Brief check: Which layer helps identify high ground?
Listen for: An elevation or relief layer.

Boundaries and symbols need interpretation

On screen: A border need not follow a ridge. / A city dot marks location, not exact city size.

Some boundaries follow natural features, while others do not. We must compare their positions instead of assuming every border is a mountain ridge or river. Point symbols also simplify information. A large city dot may be drawn for visibility and does not necessarily show the city’s actual area. Explain the difference between a symbol’s function and its physical appearance. Careful map reading uses the legend, scale and layers together. It avoids converting a convenient drawing convention into an unsupported statement about the ground.

Brief check: Does a large city dot necessarily show the city’s ground area?
Listen for: No. It may be a point symbol chosen for visibility.

7B · Week 4 · Lesson 1 · sections 3.3

40-minute route: recall 4, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 8, worked example 5, practice 10, check 5, exit 3. Divide each section between the topics in combined lessons. Timings are estimates.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

Can one cold day tell us a place’s climate?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. No. Weather describes a short period; climate needs observations over many years. Connect this to today’s task: Two weather stations.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can compare weather measurements without calling them climate.

On screen: Today’s task: Two weather stations / You will make a weather comparison or rainfall process diagram. / Compare measurements from the same period. / Link rising moist air, cooling and condensation. / Distinguish a day’s weather from long-term climate.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: a weather comparison or rainfall process diagram. Explain the three criteria: Compare measurements from the same period. Link rising moist air, cooling and condensation. Distinguish a day’s weather from long-term climate. The independent task uses this case: Invented day: West 12°C,18 mm; East 14°C,4 mm.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Weather: Atmospheric conditions at a particular time. Today’s temperature and rainfall. / Climate: Typical weather over many years. Compare typical conditions across many years. / Rainfall: Rain measured over a stated period. 18 mm in a day is not a climate average.

Weather: Atmospheric conditions at a particular time. Example: Today’s temperature and rainfall. Climate: Typical weather over many years. Example: Compare typical conditions across many years. Rainfall: Rain measured over a stated period. Example: 18 mm in a day is not a climate average. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Weather and climate use different time scales

On screen: Weather: conditions at a time and place. / Climate: long-term patterns of weather.

Weather describes conditions such as temperature, rainfall and wind at a particular time and place. Climate describes their long-term patterns and variation. A rainy afternoon is weather; it does not by itself establish a place’s typical rainfall. Show two station readings and state their dates before comparing them. Then explain why many observations across years are needed to investigate climate. Avoid saying that weather is random or that climate never changes. They concern related atmospheric conditions examined over different time scales.

Brief check: Does one cold day prove a cold climate?
Listen for: No. Climate needs long-term observations.

Read the measurements and units

On screen: Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius here. / Rainfall is measured in millimetres here.

A temperature value and a rainfall value measure different things. Degrees Celsius describe temperature; rainfall depth in millimetres describes an amount over the stated period. Read the station, date, unit and observation period before comparing numbers. Ten millimetres recorded in one hour cannot be interpreted in the same way as ten millimetres spread across a month. Compare like measurements over like periods. A weather table can show which station was wetter in the exercise without proving why that difference occurred.

Brief check: What must be checked besides the rainfall number?
Listen for: The unit, location and period over which it was recorded.

Mountains can force moist air to rise

On screen: Air rises on the windward side. / Rising air cools; cloud and rain can form.

Wind brings air towards a mountain. On the side facing the incoming wind, moist air is forced upwards. As the air rises, it expands and cools. Cooling can allow water vapour to condense into cloud droplets, and precipitation may result. Trace the rising arrow, then point to the cloud and rain. The sequence connects the mountain, air movement and rainfall rather than merely saying that mountains are wet. Windward describes the side facing the incoming wind, so that side can change when the wind direction changes.

Brief check: What happens to the air as it rises in this explanation?
Listen for: It cools, helping cloud droplets form.

The leeward side may be drier

On screen: Leeward is away from the incoming wind. / Descending air warms; a rain shadow may form.

After crossing the high ground, air can descend on the leeward side. Descending air warms, which can reduce relative humidity and discourage cloud formation. This helps explain a rain-shadow pattern. It does not mean that the leeward side can never receive rain: other weather systems and conditions also matter. Reverse the wind arrow and reconsider which side is windward. In the UK, western uplands often enhance rainfall from moist westerly air, but a simplified diagram does not predict every day’s weather at every station.

Brief check: If the wind reverses, must the windward side stay the same?
Listen for: No. It is defined by the incoming wind direction.

Then give pupils the different case on the next step.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Weather: Atmospheric conditions at a particular time. Today’s temperature and rainfall. / Climate: Typical weather over many years. Compare typical conditions across many years. / Rainfall: Rain measured over a stated period. 18 mm in a day is not a climate average.

Weather: Atmospheric conditions at a particular time. Example: Today’s temperature and rainfall. Climate: Typical weather over many years. Example: Compare typical conditions across many years. Rainfall: Rain measured over a stated period. Example: 18 mm in a day is not a climate average. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Weather and climate use different time scales

On screen: Weather: conditions at a time and place. / Climate: long-term patterns of weather.

Weather describes conditions such as temperature, rainfall and wind at a particular time and place. Climate describes their long-term patterns and variation. A rainy afternoon is weather; it does not by itself establish a place’s typical rainfall. Show two station readings and state their dates before comparing them. Then explain why many observations across years are needed to investigate climate. Avoid saying that weather is random or that climate never changes. They concern related atmospheric conditions examined over different time scales.

Brief check: Does one cold day prove a cold climate?
Listen for: No. Climate needs long-term observations.

Read the measurements and units

On screen: Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius here. / Rainfall is measured in millimetres here.

A temperature value and a rainfall value measure different things. Degrees Celsius describe temperature; rainfall depth in millimetres describes an amount over the stated period. Read the station, date, unit and observation period before comparing numbers. Ten millimetres recorded in one hour cannot be interpreted in the same way as ten millimetres spread across a month. Compare like measurements over like periods. A weather table can show which station was wetter in the exercise without proving why that difference occurred.

Brief check: What must be checked besides the rainfall number?
Listen for: The unit, location and period over which it was recorded.

Mountains can force moist air to rise

On screen: Air rises on the windward side. / Rising air cools; cloud and rain can form.

Wind brings air towards a mountain. On the side facing the incoming wind, moist air is forced upwards. As the air rises, it expands and cools. Cooling can allow water vapour to condense into cloud droplets, and precipitation may result. Trace the rising arrow, then point to the cloud and rain. The sequence connects the mountain, air movement and rainfall rather than merely saying that mountains are wet. Windward describes the side facing the incoming wind, so that side can change when the wind direction changes.

Brief check: What happens to the air as it rises in this explanation?
Listen for: It cools, helping cloud droplets form.

The leeward side may be drier

On screen: Leeward is away from the incoming wind. / Descending air warms; a rain shadow may form.

After crossing the high ground, air can descend on the leeward side. Descending air warms, which can reduce relative humidity and discourage cloud formation. This helps explain a rain-shadow pattern. It does not mean that the leeward side can never receive rain: other weather systems and conditions also matter. Reverse the wind arrow and reconsider which side is windward. In the UK, western uplands often enhance rainfall from moist westerly air, but a simplified diagram does not predict every day’s weather at every station.

Brief check: If the wind reverses, must the windward side stay the same?
Listen for: No. It is defined by the incoming wind direction.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Population: People living in a defined area. Count residents in a defined place. / Community: People connected by place or activity. A person can join music and sports groups. / Diversity: Differences within a group. People in one town can have different interests.

Population: People living in a defined area. Example: Count residents in a defined place. Community: People connected by place or activity. Example: A person can join music and sports groups. Diversity: Differences within a group. Example: People in one town can have different interests. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Population, community and identity

On screen: Population: people living in an area. / People can belong to several communities.

A population is the people living in a defined area. It contains individuals with different ages, experiences, backgrounds and interests. A community can be connected by place or by shared activities, while identity concerns how people understand themselves and their connections. These groups can overlap: someone can belong to a local neighbourhood, a language community and a sports club. The UK is not one uniform group of people who all have the same experiences or preferences. Nor should we assume that every member of a cultural group thinks alike. When we examine population information, ask which aspect was measured. A hobby survey tells us about hobbies in its sample; it does not establish someone’s whole identity or describe all people in the country.

Brief check: Can one person belong to several communities?
Listen for: Yes. Communities and identities can overlap.

Describe diversity without stereotyping

On screen: Culture includes practices, language and traditions. / A group label does not predict every individual.

Culture includes shared practices, languages, traditions and ways of expressing meaning. Cultures change and can interact, while individuals participate in them differently. Use everyday examples such as different celebrations, foods or languages without ranking them or assuming everyone in a country follows one tradition. Population data can describe a distribution when it has a defined source and category, but cannot tell us every individual’s opinions. Distinguish a careful statement about a measured group from a stereotype. If we ask a small group about music or sport, report its actual responses and overlap. Do not turn that exercise into a statement that every person in the UK likes the same things.

Brief check: Does a community label establish each member’s favourite activity?
Listen for: No. Individuals within a community can differ.

People and data are not the same thing

On screen: Population: the group we want to describe. / Sample: the people we actually study.

Population can mean the total people in an area or, in a survey, the whole group we want to learn about. A sample is the smaller group actually studied. If we ask ten residents, we know their answers; we have not automatically heard from every resident. Explain why surveys use samples and why selection matters. Volunteers from one club may share interests that differ from other residents. A larger sample can still be biased if it repeatedly selects the same narrow kind of participant.

Brief check: Does asking more members of one club guarantee a representative sample?
Listen for: No. The selection may still be restricted.

Counts and proportions answer different questions

On screen: Count: how many? / Proportion: how many out of the total?

A count tells us the number in a category. A proportion relates that number to the whole group. Six out of ten is a larger proportion than twelve out of thirty, even though twelve is the larger count. Use groups of drawn people to show the numerator and denominator before calculating percentages. The question determines which comparison is useful. Counts can matter for service demand, while proportions help compare groups of different sizes. Neither should be substituted for the other without explaining the change.

Brief check: Which has the higher proportion: 6 of 10 or 12 of 30?
Listen for: 6 of 10: 60%, compared with 40%.

Overlapping groups need care

On screen: A person can belong to two groups. / Do not count the overlap twice in the total.

Suppose some pupils both walk and cycle on different days. Adding the walking count and cycling count may count those pupils twice. Draw two overlapping circles and put the shared pupils in the middle. To find the number in at least one group, add both counts and subtract the overlap once. Explain that the categories and question must be clear before calculating. A survey about usual travel mode may use different rules from a survey asking every mode used during the week.

Brief check: Why can adding two group counts overestimate the number of people?
Listen for: Some people may belong to both groups.

Write a headline that fits the survey

On screen: Name who was asked. / Do not turn a sample into “everyone”.

A headline should reflect the evidence’s scope. If a survey asks cycling-club volunteers, report their responses rather than claiming all residents have the same views. Explain how a word such as everyone can make a statement much stronger than the data support. Keep useful findings while correcting the population claim. A careful geographical report includes the sample, question and relevant period. It can also say which other groups should be studied before making a wider conclusion about the town.

Brief check: How should a limited survey’s headline be qualified?
Listen for: Name the sampled group rather than claiming it describes everyone.
