On screen: Watch your teacher demonstrate one move. / One volunteer can come to the board; everyone else watches.

Introduce the rule before making a move. Sandpaper sliding over a surface models scraping better than a smooth block, but real erosion also depends on pressure, speed, rock and debris. Change one model factor at a time to make a fair comparison. Explain why one choice fits and why the other does not. Holding other conditions constant makes the effect of the changed factor easier to interpret. Then invite a volunteer for one turn if useful. Take one brief response from the class and finish by restating the geographical idea. This is the one core board activity for this topic; the teacher may operate it throughout.

On screen: Predict which better illustrates abrasion. / Explain why this is not a complete prediction of real erosion rates.

Pupils create a rock-journey storyboard using the displayed evidence. Task: Predict which better illustrates abrasion. Explain why this is not a complete prediction of real erosion rates. Listen for: B has abrasive material. Real erosion also depends on speed, pressure, temperature and rock conditions. Allow independent work before comparing. Do not invent missing data. Accept different justified responses where the case allows them.

Check and improve your a rock-journey storyboard

On screen: Distinguish plucking from abrasion. / Show removal, transport and scraping. / Explain one correction or useful addition to your partner.

Partners compare their work with the evidence, not just each other’s answers. Check Distinguish plucking from abrasion. Show removal, transport and scraping. Explain which conditions a comparison keeps constant. In combined lessons, each partner chooses a different investigation. Keep the original response and explain one revision.

Share a result and explain it

On screen: Show one result from Two glaciers, different tools. / Explain how the evidence supports it, using show removal, transport and scraping.

Invite two short explanations, preferably different methods or conclusions. Check each against its case source. Expected reasoning for the final case: B has abrasive material. Real erosion also depends on speed, pressure, temperature and rock conditions.

Which action is plucking?

On screen:

Collect an independent explanation using this new source. Do not reveal until pupils have attempted it. Listen for: Ice removes a loosened block from the bed or side. Accept equivalent justified wording.

What happens when ice melts and releases the debris?

On screen:

Collect an independent explanation using this new source. Do not reveal until pupils have attempted it. Listen for: Deposition: the carried material is left behind. Accept equivalent justified wording.

Change the valley shape

7B · Week 21 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.4

40-minute route: recall 4, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 8, worked example 5, practice 10, check 5, exit 3. Divide each section between the topics in combined lessons. Timings are estimates.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

Is a river bend viewed from above evidence of a U-shaped valley?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. No. Valley shape is a cross-section across the valley, not the river’s plan-view bend. Connect this to today’s task: Change the valley shape.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can explain widening and deepening in cross-section.

On screen: Today’s task: Change the valley shape / You will make matched valley sketches. / Compare a V-shaped section with a glacial trough. / Show widening and deepening by ice. / Distinguish plan view from cross-section.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: matched valley sketches. Explain the three criteria: Compare a V-shaped section with a glacial trough. Show widening and deepening by ice. Distinguish plan view from cross-section. The independent task uses this case: Compare a narrow V-shaped river-valley cross-section with a glacial trough: a broad floor and steep sides. Draw slices across the valleys, not a river bend viewed from above.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: U-shaped valley: A broad, steep-sided valley shaped by ice. Compare a broad floor and steep sides. / Hanging valley: A tributary valley above the main valley floor. A tributary joins above the main valley floor. / Truncated spur: A ridge end cut short by moving ice. Ice cuts across the end of a ridge.

U-shaped valley: A broad, steep-sided valley shaped by ice. Example: Compare a broad floor and steep sides. Hanging valley: A tributary valley above the main valley floor. Example: A tributary joins above the main valley floor. Truncated spur: A ridge end cut short by moving ice. Example: Ice cuts across the end of a ridge. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Hanging valleys show different erosion levels

On screen: A tributary valley can meet a deeper main trough. / Its floor may remain above the main valley floor.

A smaller tributary glacier may erode less deeply than a larger glacier in the main valley. After the ice disappears, the tributary valley floor can lie above the deeper main trough. This is called a hanging valley. Trace the two floors and their height difference. A stream may drop from the higher tributary towards the lower main floor, sometimes creating a waterfall. The explanation concerns different amounts of erosion in connected valleys; it is not a valley floating without support. Use the cross-section or a suitable diagram to show the relationship clearly before introducing the name. The landform joins local shapes to the wider glacier system that once occupied the valleys.

Brief check: Why can the tributary valley floor lie above the main floor?
Listen for: The main glacier may have eroded its valley more deeply.

Truncated spurs mark altered valley sides

On screen: Ridges can project into an earlier valley. / Glacial erosion can cut back their ends.

A spur is a ridge projecting from a valley side. A river valley may wind around interlocking spurs, while a large glacier moving through the valley can erode their projecting ends. The cut-back faces are called truncated spurs. Show a plan view with projecting ridges before the altered trough. Explain why this landform needs a different view from a simple profile across the floor. It helps pupils connect three-dimensional landscape features rather than treating every glacial feature as the same letter-shaped cross-section. In a real landscape, suitable evidence is needed to identify the shape and its history; the schematic clarifies the proposed mechanism.

Brief check: What part of the spur is described as truncated?
Listen for: Its projecting end has been cut back.

A valley cross-section looks across

On screen: Compare the floor and both sides. / The viewing direction matters.

A cross-section shows the shape across a valley rather than along its length. Mark one side, the floor and the other side. A photograph looking down the valley may not reveal that profile clearly, so source choice matters. A river and glacier can both occupy a valley without producing the same typical cross-section. Begin with description: is the floor narrow or broad, and how do the sides rise? Then connect the form to the processes that may have modified it, using suitable evidence.

Brief check: Which view best tests a cross-section claim?
Listen for: A view or profile across the valley.

River valleys are often V-shaped

On screen: River erosion cuts into the valley floor. / Slope processes affect the sides.

Many upper river valleys have narrow floors and sloping sides, giving a V-shaped cross-section. Downward river erosion and material moving from the sides both contribute to the form. Explain that the letter is a simplified description, not an exact geometry found everywhere. Other factors such as rock, structure and past processes affect actual valleys. Point to the narrow channel and the slopes so pupils understand what the label describes. A V shape is a useful pattern for comparison rather than proof that one agent explains the entire history.

Brief check: What part of a typical V-shaped profile is narrow?
Listen for: The valley floor.

Glaciers widen and deepen valleys

On screen: Ice occupies much of the valley. / Erosion can make a broad trough.

A valley glacier can occupy a large part of a valley rather than being confined to a narrow water channel. Erosion at the bed and sides can deepen and widen the valley, producing a glacial trough with a broad floor and steep sides. The common U-shaped label summarises that cross-section. Trace the contact areas before showing the changed profile. Do not say ice merely sits in the valley and leaves the shape unchanged. The form results from interaction between moving ice, carried debris and the rock it encounters.

Brief check: Why can ice affect more of the valley profile than a narrow channel?
Listen for: A glacier can occupy and erode a much broader part of the valley.

Describe the form before claiming the cause

On screen: Broad floor and steep sides describe shape. / Further evidence supports the glacial history.

A pupil can correctly describe a broad floor without yet proving its origin. Link the description to a process explanation, then identify evidence that would support past glacier activity. Compare a suitable cross-profile with a view along the floor and explain why one source answers the shape question more directly. Real valleys can have complex histories and later river changes. A useful answer states the form observed, the proposed process and the evidence available, instead of using the word glacier as a substitute for explanation.

Brief check: Does every broad valley photograph prove a complete glacial history?
Listen for: No. Use appropriate additional evidence.

Demonstrate this complete example: Draw the valley as if sliced across. River erosion can form a narrow V; glacial erosion can widen the floor and steepen sides into a trough. Arrows should point at the surfaces removed, not imply ice deposits the valley. Explain each operation or causal link aloud. Then give pupils the different case on the next step.

Arrows should point at the surfaces removed, not imply ice deposits the valley. Explain why one choice fits and why the other does not. Cross-section displays floor width and side slopes directly. Then invite a volunteer for one turn if useful. Take one brief response from the class and finish by restating the geographical idea. This is the one core board activity for this topic; the teacher may operate it throughout.

Partners compare their work with the evidence, not just each other’s answers. Check Compare a V-shaped section with a glacial trough. Show widening and deepening by ice. Distinguish plan view from cross-section. In combined lessons, each partner chooses a different investigation. Keep the original response and explain one revision.

Share a result and explain it

On screen: Show one result from Change the valley shape. / Explain how the evidence supports it, using show widening and deepening by ice.

Invite two short explanations, preferably different methods or conclusions. Check each against its case source. Expected reasoning for the final case: Ice erosion widens the sides and deepens the floor, producing a broader cross-section.

On screen:

Collect an independent explanation using this new source. Do not reveal until pupils have attempted it. Listen for: A cross-section cuts across the valley. Accept equivalent justified wording.

Does “U-shaped” mean the valley follows a U on a map?

On screen:

Carve a mountain

7B · Week 22 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.5

40-minute route: recall 4, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 8, worked example 5, practice 10, check 5, exit 3. Divide each section between the topics in combined lessons. Timings are estimates.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

How is a corrie different from an arête?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. A corrie is a hollow; an arête is a narrow ridge left between eroded hollows or valleys. Connect this to today’s task: Carve a mountain.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can explain a corrie and the ridge between hollows.

On screen: Today’s task: Carve a mountain / You will make a labelled mountain diagram or guidebook description. / Locate hollows, back walls and ridges. / Explain erosion on different sides. / Connect the remaining shape to the process.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: a labelled mountain diagram or guidebook description. Explain the three criteria: Locate hollows, back walls and ridges. Explain erosion on different sides. Connect the remaining shape to the process. The independent task uses this case: The model places two growing hollows on opposite sides of a ridge.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Corrie: An armchair-shaped hollow carved by ice. A bowl-shaped mountain hollow. / Arête: A sharp ridge between glacial hollows. A narrow ridge between two hollows. / Pyramidal peak: A pointed peak eroded from several sides. Erosion from several sides sharpens a peak.

Corrie: An armchair-shaped hollow carved by ice. Example: A bowl-shaped mountain hollow. Arête: A sharp ridge between glacial hollows. Example: A narrow ridge between two hollows. Pyramidal peak: A pointed peak eroded from several sides. Example: Erosion from several sides sharpens a peak. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

A corrie is a mountain hollow

On screen: A corrie is a bowl-like hollow. / Ice can erode its bed and back wall.

A corrie, also called a cirque, is a bowl-like hollow in a mountain landscape. Snow can collect in a suitable hollow and develop into ice. Erosion can deepen the floor and steepen the back wall, while a rock lip may remain towards the entrance. Point to these parts separately so the word names a landform rather than any mountain lake. Water may occupy a corrie after the ice has gone, but a lake is not required for the hollow to be identified.

Brief check: Is the corrie the ridge or the hollow?
Listen for: The hollow.

An arête is a sharp ridge

On screen: Erosion acts on neighbouring hollows. / A narrow ridge can remain between them.

An arête is a narrow, sharp ridge. When neighbouring corries or glacial valleys erode towards a divide, the ridge between them can become sharper. Show two eroded hollows and trace the remaining high ground. The arête is the material left between the erosion areas, not the bowl itself. This explains why correct labels depend on the part of the landscape being named. Use a finger or pointer to distinguish hollow, wall and ridge before expecting pupils to recall the terminology.

Brief check: Which feature remains between neighbouring eroded hollows?
Listen for: An arête.

Several ridges can meet at a peak

On screen: Erosion can act on several sides. / A sharp peak may remain between them.

Where erosion works around a mountain from several directions, a sharply pointed peak can remain. The common term pyramidal peak describes this form. Compare it with an arête: one is a peak, the other a ridge. Trace each in the diagram and explain how they connect to surrounding hollows. A schematic makes the relationships easier to see but does not prove the complete origin of every real pointed mountain. Rock structure and other processes also affect actual shapes, so apply the terms using relevant landscape evidence.

Brief check: How is a peak different from a ridge?
Listen for: A peak is a summit; a ridge is an extended line of high ground.

Connect each name to the process

On screen: Corrie: hollow. Arête: ridge. / Peak: summit left between eroded areas.

Return to the whole mountain after teaching its parts. Point to one feature and describe its position relative to the others. Then explain which areas were eroded and which high ground remained. This prevents a list of unfamiliar words from replacing understanding. A good description locates the feature, while a good explanation connects it to erosion around it. If a pupil labels the hollow arête, correct the part of the landscape being named rather than merely repeating the vocabulary louder.

Brief check: Why is labelling a hollow “arête” incorrect?
Listen for: The arête is the ridge; the hollow is the corrie.

17–22 min · Worked example

Worked example · Carve a mountain

On screen: Locate hollows, back walls and ridges. / Explain erosion on different sides.

Demonstrate this complete example: A corrie is an armchair-like hollow shaped by glacial erosion, with a steep back wall. When neighbouring hollows erode back towards each other, a narrow ridge can remain between them: an arête. Explain each operation or causal link aloud. Then give pupils the different case on the next step.

What does an arête describe?

On screen:

Use the worked example’s method on this different case. Invite pupils’ reasoning before showing: A narrow ridge between eroded hollows or valleys. The feature is the remaining ridge, not the hollow or a sediment pile.

Class board challenge · Explain a corrie and the ridge between hollows

On screen: Watch your teacher demonstrate one move. / One volunteer can come to the board; everyone else watches.

Introduce the rule before making a move. A corrie is an armchair-like hollow shaped by glacial erosion, with a steep back wall. When neighbouring hollows erode back towards each other, a narrow ridge can remain between them: an arête. Explain why one choice fits and why the other does not. The feature is the remaining ridge, not the hollow or a sediment pile. Then invite a volunteer for one turn if useful. Words for today

On screen: Corrie: An armchair-shaped hollow carved by ice. A bowl-shaped mountain hollow. / Arête: A sharp ridge between glacial hollows. A narrow ridge between two hollows. / Pyramidal peak: A pointed peak eroded from several sides. Erosion from several sides sharpens a peak.

Pyramidal peak: A pointed peak eroded from several sides. Example: Erosion from several sides sharpens a peak. Point to the relevant part of each picture. 9–17 min · Teacher explanation

A corrie is a mountain hollow

On screen: A corrie is a bowl-like hollow. / Ice can erode its bed and back wall.

A corrie, also called a cirque, is a bowl-like hollow in a mountain landscape. Snow can collect in a suitable hollow and develop into ice. Erosion can deepen the floor and steepen the back wall, while a rock lip may remain towards the entrance. Point to these parts separately so the word names a landform rather than any mountain lake. Water may occupy a corrie after the ice has gone, but a lake is not required for the hollow to be identified.

Brief check: Is the corrie the ridge or the hollow?
Listen for: The hollow.

An arête is a sharp ridge

On screen: Erosion acts on neighbouring hollows. / A narrow ridge can remain between them.

An arête is a narrow, sharp ridge. When neighbouring corries or glacial valleys erode towards a divide, the ridge between them can become sharper. Show two eroded hollows and trace the remaining high ground. The arête is the material left between the erosion areas, not the bowl itself. This explains why correct labels depend on the part of the landscape being named. Use a finger or pointer to distinguish hollow, wall and ridge before expecting pupils to recall the terminology.

Brief check: Which feature remains between neighbouring eroded hollows?
Listen for: An arête.

Several ridges can meet at a peak

On screen: Erosion can act on several sides. / A sharp peak may remain between them.

Where erosion works around a mountain from several directions, a sharply pointed peak can remain. The common term pyramidal peak describes this form. Compare it with an arête: one is a peak, the other a ridge. Trace each in the diagram and explain how they connect to surrounding hollows. A schematic makes the relationships easier to see but does not prove the complete origin of every real pointed mountain. Rock structure and other processes also affect actual shapes, so apply the terms using relevant landscape evidence.

Brief check: How is a peak different from a ridge?
Listen for: A peak is a summit; a ridge is an extended line of high ground.

Connect each name to the process

On screen: Corrie: hollow. Arête: ridge. / Peak: summit left between eroded areas.

Return to the whole mountain after teaching its parts. Point to one feature and describe its position relative to the others. Then explain which areas were eroded and which high ground remained. This prevents a list of unfamiliar words from replacing understanding. A good description locates the feature, while a good explanation connects it to erosion around it. If a pupil labels the hollow arête, correct the part of the landscape being named rather than merely repeating the vocabulary louder.

Brief check: Why is labelling a hollow “arête” incorrect?
Listen for: The arête is the ridge; the hollow is the corrie.

What the ice leaves behind

7B · Week 23 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.6

40-minute route: recall 4, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 8, worked example 5, practice 10, check 5, exit 3. Divide each section between the topics in combined lessons. Timings are estimates.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

Does glacier ice always sort its deposits by particle size?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. No. Till commonly contains mixed particle sizes released together as ice melts. Connect this to today’s task: What the ice leaves behind.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can explain deposition when ice loses its load.

On screen: Today’s task: What the ice leaves behind / You will make a deposit sketch and cautious reconstruction. / Show mixed sizes in till. / Relate debris accumulations to ice margins. / Name evidence needed to confirm former extent.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: a deposit sketch and cautious reconstruction. Explain the three criteria: Show mixed sizes in till. Relate debris accumulations to ice margins. Name evidence needed to confirm former extent. The independent task uses this case: Model load: clay, sand, pebbles and boulders. Ice melts at its margin.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Deposition: Material being dropped. Melting ice releases its debris. / Till: Unsorted material deposited by ice. Clay, sand and boulders are mixed together. / Moraine: A build-up of debris carried or deposited by a glacier. Debris can build a ridge at an ice margin.

Deposition: Material being dropped. Example: Melting ice releases its debris. Till: Unsorted material deposited by ice. Example: Clay, sand and boulders are mixed together. Moraine: A build-up of debris carried or deposited by a glacier. Example: Debris can build a ridge at an ice margin. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Erratics link deposits to transport

On screen: An erratic differs from the local bedrock. / Its rock type can help investigate where it came from.

A glacial erratic is a transported rock that differs from the local bedrock where it now lies. Its presence can prompt a question about movement from another source area. Compare the rock type with surrounding ground, then investigate a possible matching source and evidence of glacial transport. Difference alone should be interpreted in context rather than used as complete proof of every detail of a journey. An erratic connects the three stages of removal, transport and deposition: the rock began somewhere, moved and was left behind. It also differs from a moraine, which is an accumulation of debris rather than the name for one particular transported block.

Brief check: How does an erratic differ from local bedrock?
Listen for: It has been transported and is of a different rock type from the surrounding bedrock.

Glaciers transport debris

On screen: Material can travel on, within or beneath ice. / Transport differs from its original removal.

Glaciers can carry material in several positions: on the surface, within the ice or near the bed. Rock may enter from erosion beneath the glacier or from valley sides. Removal, transport and deposition are distinct stages. A fragment can be eroded in one place and deposited elsewhere after a period of movement. Trace one fragment through this sequence. Its final location therefore does not automatically show where it originated. This distinction helps explain why deposited material can provide clues about past glacier movement.

Brief check: Does a deposited fragment necessarily come from the place where it now lies?
Listen for: No. It may have been transported.

Deposition leaves material behind

On screen: Melting ice releases carried debris. / Direct glacial deposits can be poorly sorted.

When debris-bearing ice melts, its carried material can be left behind. Directly deposited glacial material, often called till, commonly contains a mixture of particle sizes rather than neatly separated layers. Explain why ice can carry fine and coarse material together. A simple mixed pile models that idea, but real deposits vary and need field evidence. Do not use poor sorting as the only possible clue or assume every mixed deposit is glacial. Interpret it alongside location, landforms and other geological information.

Brief check: What does “poorly sorted” mean here?
Listen for: Different particle sizes are mixed together.

Moraines mark accumulations of debris

On screen: Some lie along glacier sides. / Others form near the front or where ice streams meet.

A moraine is an accumulation of glacial debris. Lateral moraines lie along glacier sides. Where glacier streams join, debris from their adjacent margins can form a medial moraine. Accumulations near an end position include terminal or end moraines. Use location to distinguish the names instead of treating them as separate kinds of rock. A ridge of debris may help reconstruct a former ice margin, but interpreting its age and origin needs appropriate evidence. The visible position is the starting observation, not the entire historical conclusion.

Brief check: What helps distinguish lateral and end moraines?
Listen for: Their positions relative to the glacier.

Meltwater can sort sediment

On screen: Moving water carries different sizes differently. / Sorted layers may reflect meltwater deposition.

Meltwater flows away from ice and can transport and deposit sediment. Flowing water can sort particles because different sizes and densities settle under different conditions. A strongly layered, sorted deposit therefore raises a different interpretation from a simple direct release of mixed debris by melting ice. Location near a glacier does not mean every deposit was laid down directly by ice. Compare the mechanisms and ask which observations each predicts. The answer should match the deposit’s features and context rather than rely only on the region’s label.

Brief check: What alternative should we consider for sorted sediment near a glacier?
Listen for: Transport and deposition by meltwater.

A valley visitor plan

7B · Week 24 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.7

40-minute route: recall 4, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 8, worked example 5, practice 10, check 5, exit 3. Divide each section between the topics in combined lessons. Timings are estimates.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

Can tourism bring benefits and environmental pressure at the same time?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. Yes. Visitors can support jobs and access while also wearing paths or affecting habitats. Connect this to today’s task: A valley visitor plan.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can connect landform, visitors and measurable pressure.

On screen: Today’s task: A valley visitor plan / You will make a visitor management proposal. / Explain how the landscape affects routes. / Compare visitor counts for the stated period. / Propose management and evidence to test it.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: a visitor management proposal. Explain the three criteria: Explain how the landscape affects routes. Compare visitor counts for the stated period. Propose management and evidence to test it. The independent task uses this case: Langdale is a Lake District glacial valley. Classroom path counts: A 80 visitors/hour, B 20. A broad floor and steep sides are features of a glacial trough.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Glacial landscape: Land with features shaped by ice. A broad glacial valley attracts walkers. / Tourism: Travel to places for visits. Visitor counts describe use for a stated time. / Conservation: Protecting valued places and habitats. Path repair can help protect the landscape.

Glacial landscape: Land with features shaped by ice. Example: A broad glacial valley attracts walkers. Tourism: Travel to places for visits. Example: Visitor counts describe use for a stated time. Conservation: Protecting valued places and habitats. Example: Path repair can help protect the landscape. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

A glacial valley can become a visitor landscape

On screen: Broad floors and steep sides affect movement. / The landform remains after ice retreats.

A glacial trough can provide striking scenery and routes through mountain country after its glacier disappears. A broad floor and steep sides affect where paths, roads and settlements can lie. Langdale in the Lake District provides a named example of a glacial valley landscape, while the visitor counts in our exercises are fictional. Separate the real place and landform from invented measurements. Explain how physical geography shapes opportunities and constraints for people rather than treating landscape and tourism as unrelated topics.

Brief check: How can steep sides affect visitor movement?
Listen for: They can limit suitable routes and access.

Visitors create benefits and pressures

On screen: Visitors can support local businesses. / Concentrated use can affect paths and habitats.

Visitors may support accommodation, shops, guiding and other local services. Repeated foot traffic can also wear paths, disturb sensitive areas and create waste or congestion. Explain the mechanism behind each effect. More people walking on a path can increase pressure, but visitor numbers alone do not establish its damage level. Surface, weather and maintenance matter too. A balanced account recognises benefits and costs without assuming that tourism is always either harmful or beneficial in every place and under every condition.

Brief check: Do visitor counts alone measure path damage?
Listen for: No. We need information about condition and other relevant factors.

A snapshot needs a context

On screen: Counts need a time and place. / Repeat counts before describing a general pattern.

Eighty visitors on one path and twenty on another describe the observation period in the source. They do not prove the first is always four times busier. Check whether counts cover equal times and comparable locations, then consider day, season and weather. Repeat observations to investigate variation. The same number of visitors can also affect different habitats differently. Use the figures to raise a management question while avoiding a conclusion that goes beyond what was measured. Geographical decisions join counts to the places in which they occur.

Brief check: What must be equal for a simple count comparison?
Listen for: The observation periods and counting rules should be comparable.

Management must consider sensitivity

On screen: A quiet path may still be fragile. / Compare access, habitat and maintenance.

Sending visitors from a crowded path to a quiet one may reduce pressure at the first location but create harm at the second. Low use does not establish unlimited capacity. Examine habitat sensitivity, route surface, accessibility and maintenance needs before recommending diversion. Measures might include repairing a surface, clearer signs, seasonal protection or directing use towards suitable routes. Each should be connected to the problem it addresses. Ask who benefits and what new pressure may be created, rather than selecting a measure because it sounds generally environmentally friendly.

Brief check: Should every spare visitor be sent to the quieter path?
Listen for: No. Check its sensitivity and capacity first.

7B · Week 24 · Lesson 2 · sections 4.8

0–4 min · Starter and recall

Does more meltwater today guarantee more water forever?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. No. A shrinking ice store may release more water now but cannot sustain that contribution indefinitely. Connect this to today’s task: A water-store budget.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can model a glacier as a changing water store.

On screen: Today’s task: A water-store budget / You will make a water-store budget and explanation. / Calculate the change in the ice store. / Separate storage from flowing water. / Compare short-term benefits and longer-term limits.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: a water-store budget and explanation. Explain the three criteria: Calculate the change in the ice store. Separate storage from flowing water. Compare short-term benefits and longer-term limits. The independent task uses this case: Invented ice store 100 units; addition 8, loss 12 in one year.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Meltwater: Water produced when ice melts. Melting ice feeds a stream. / Storage: Water held in a place or form. Ice holds water before it is released. / Water balance: The difference between water inputs and outputs. Inputs minus outputs change the store.

Meltwater: Water produced when ice melts. Example: Melting ice feeds a stream. Storage: Water held in a place or form. Example: Ice holds water before it is released. Water balance: The difference between water inputs and outputs. Example: Inputs minus outputs change the store. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Ice is a water store

On screen: Snow and ice hold water over time. / Melting releases water to other stores and flows.

A glacier stores water as ice. Snowfall can add to that store, while melting can release liquid water. A store is an amount held at a time; a flow is movement into or out of it. Show a storage box with incoming and outgoing arrows. This distinction helps us understand why a large river flow does not necessarily mean the ice store is growing. Water in the river may come from rainfall as well as melting. Follow each input separately before making a claim about the stored ice.

Brief check: Is river flow the same quantity as water stored in ice?
Listen for: No. One is a flow and the other a store.

Water can have several inputs

On screen: Rainfall can contribute to runoff. / Snowmelt and ice melt can also contribute.

A mountain river can receive rainfall runoff, snowmelt, glacier melt and other contributions. Their importance varies through time and between basins. In the classroom model, label the separate arrows rather than combining them into an unexplained total. A wet year may increase river flow even while glacier mass decreases. To explain an observed change, identify which inputs were measured and which were not. The question is not simply whether a glacier exists nearby, but how water reaches the river under the stated conditions.

Brief check: Can extra rainfall increase flow while stored ice falls?
Listen for: Yes. Several inputs can affect river flow.

Net loss can release stored water

On screen: Losses can exceed additions. / A high outflow does not prove a growing store.

Suppose a model receives eight units and releases twelve during the same period. It has used four units from storage, so its stored amount decreases. Write additions minus losses and connect the negative balance to the storage box. This illustrates the idea without predicting exact real discharge or future trends. Melting stored ice can temporarily contribute water even while reducing the remaining ice. An increase in outflow is therefore not automatically good evidence that the store is increasing or that the same flow can continue indefinitely.

Brief check: If outflow exceeds input, what happens to storage?
Listen for: It decreases by the difference in this simplified balance.

Water supply depends on timing

On screen: People need water when and where they use it. / Seasonal patterns matter as well as annual totals.

A yearly water total can conceal periods of shortage or high flow. Households, farming, hydropower and ecosystems may need water at different times. Explain why changes in snow and ice storage can alter the timing of release, not merely the total amount. A recommendation needs seasonal flow information and demand, while long-term predictions require more than one classroom calculation. Separate measured trends from a single unusual year. This connects the physical water system to human needs without pretending the simple diagram includes every management factor.

Brief check: Why is an annual total alone insufficient for supply planning?
Listen for: It can hide when water is available and when it is needed.

Use the worked example’s method on this different case. Invite pupils’ reasoning before showing: 45 units. 50 + 4 - 9 = 45; losses leave the store.

Then invite a volunteer for one turn if useful. Take one brief response from the class and finish by restating the geographical idea. Does downstream always mean towards the bottom of a map?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. No. It means in the direction of river flow towards the mouth. Connect this to today’s task: Follow the river downstream.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can use river-network vocabulary correctly.

On screen: Today’s task: Follow the river downstream / You will make a river-network diagram. / Locate source, tributary, confluence and mouth. / Follow connected channels downstream. / Explain what else is needed to predict travel time.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Source: Where a river begins. A spring can begin a river. / Tributary: A smaller river joining another river. A smaller channel joins the main river. / Mouth: Where a river enters the sea or another water body. Follow flow to a lake, sea or other water body.

Source: Where a river begins. Example: A spring can begin a river. Tributary: A smaller river joining another river. Example: A smaller channel joins the main river. Mouth: Where a river enters the sea or another water body. Example: Follow flow to a lake, sea or other water body. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

A river has a connected course

On screen: Source: where the river begins. / Mouth: where it enters another water body.

A river carries water along a connected course from its source towards its mouth. The source is where the named river begins, while the mouth is where it enters another water body. Downstream means following the flow; upstream is towards the source against that direction. Trace the course before naming individual parts. A map may show bends and junctions, but page position alone does not define downstream. Water generally moves from higher towards lower elevation, so we must use the network and flow information rather than assume rivers always run towards the bottom of the page.

Brief check: Does downstream always mean towards the bottom of a map?
Listen for: No. Follow the river’s actual flow direction.

Tributaries join the main river

On screen: Tributary: a smaller river that joins another. / Confluence: the place where rivers meet.

A tributary contributes water to another river. The confluence is the junction where they meet. Trace one tributary into the main channel and then continue downstream. The water does not stop at the junction. This connectivity matters when explaining how rainfall, sediment or pollution from one part of the basin can affect another. The direction of movement matters: a pollutant introduced below a town does not automatically travel upstream to it in our simple flow model. Locate the entry point before tracing any claimed effect.

Brief check: What is a confluence?
Listen for: The junction where rivers meet.

A drainage basin collects water

On screen: The basin drains towards a river system. / A watershed divides neighbouring basins.

A drainage basin is the area from which water drains into a river system. Its boundary, often called a watershed or drainage divide in UK school geography, separates it from neighbouring basins. Trace water from a slope into a tributary and then the main river. Land use anywhere in the connected basin may influence water reaching the channel. The river line is therefore only part of the geographical system. Our schematic makes the network clear but does not give an exact surveyed basin boundary unless that information is supplied.

Brief check: Is the basin only the water inside the river channel?
Listen for: No. It includes the land draining towards the system.

Use a named river and a separate model

On screen: The Thames flows through London towards the North Sea. / A schematic explains connections, not exact bends.

The Thames has its source in the Cotswolds and flows through London towards its estuary and the North Sea. Locate the named places on an appropriate map. Then use the simple source-to-mouth schematic to explain tributaries and confluences. Keep its purpose clear: a straight arrow can show a connection without reproducing the river’s exact shape or distances. A named real river and a fictional exercise network can be used in the same lesson if pupils know which facts belong to which source.

Brief check: Does a simple source-to-mouth arrow show every real bend of the Thames?
Listen for: No. It is a schematic connection.

Follow the arrows downstream instead of treating every branching line as a river splitting. Explain why one choice fits and why the other does not. A confluence is a junction; a watershed is a drainage divide. Then invite a volunteer for one turn if useful. Take one brief response from the class and finish by restating the geographical idea. This is the one core board activity for this topic; the teacher may operate it throughout.

7B · Week 25 · Lesson 2 · sections 5.2

40-minute route: recall 4, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 8, worked example 5, practice 10, check 5, exit 3. Divide each section between the topics in combined lessons. Timings are estimates.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

When water evaporates, does it stop existing?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. No. Liquid water changes into water vapour and moves through the water cycle. Connect this to today’s task: Become a water drop.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can explain water-cycle arrows as changes or movements.

On screen: Today’s task: Become a water drop / You will make a water-drop route with labelled processes. / Label changes of state correctly. / Connect evaporation, condensation and precipitation. / Compare stores and surface or underground pathways.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: a water-drop route with labelled processes. Explain the three criteria: Label changes of state correctly. Connect evaporation, condensation and precipitation. Compare stores and surface or underground pathways. The independent task uses this case: Start in a lake. Your route must include evaporation, condensation, precipitation and one land pathway.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Evaporation: Liquid water becoming water vapour. Energy helps liquid water become vapour. / Condensation: Water vapour becoming liquid droplets. Cooling vapour can form cloud droplets. / Precipitation: Water falling from clouds. Rain or snow returns water to land or sea.

Evaporation: Liquid water becoming water vapour. Example: Energy helps liquid water become vapour. Condensation: Water vapour becoming liquid droplets. Example: Cooling vapour can form cloud droplets. Precipitation: Water falling from clouds. Example: Rain or snow returns water to land or sea. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Water moves between stores

On screen: Water can be stored in oceans, ice, soil and groundwater. / Processes move water between stores.

The water cycle describes water moving between places and changing state. Oceans, lakes, ice, soil and groundwater are stores. A store holds water; a process moves it or changes its form. Trace one possible route rather than suggesting that every drop follows the same circle at the same speed. Water can remain in different stores for very different times. A classroom diagram simplifies a large connected system, so its arrows should help explain specific transfers rather than become a sequence memorised without meaning.

Brief check: Is soil water a store or a transfer?
Listen for: A store.

Evaporation, condensation and precipitation

On screen: Evaporation: liquid becomes water vapour. / Condensation forms droplets; precipitation falls.

Energy can cause liquid water to become water vapour through evaporation. Vapour is a gas and is not the same as visible cloud droplets. When air cools sufficiently, condensation can form droplets or, under suitable conditions, ice particles. Precipitation includes water falling from clouds as rain, snow or other forms. Trace these processes with their correct state changes. Do not say clouds are simply invisible gas that falls unchanged. The explanation should connect energy, state and movement using accessible words before introducing the technical terms.

Brief check: Is visible cloud made only of invisible water vapour?
Listen for: No. Visible cloud contains droplets or ice particles.

Infiltration and runoff are different paths

On screen: Infiltration: water enters the ground. / Runoff: water flows over the surface.

When rain reaches land, some water may enter the soil through infiltration. Some may move across the surface as runoff. Vegetation can intercept rainfall, and stored water can later evaporate or move through the ground. The balance depends on rainfall and the condition of the surface and soil. Already saturated soil has less available storage, so further rain may produce more surface runoff. Point to the alternative arrows and explain why the same rainfall amount need not create the same rapid river response everywhere.

Brief check: What can saturation change during further rainfall?
Listen for: It can reduce additional storage and increase surface runoff.

The basin model has a boundary

On screen: A simple split can show runoff and infiltration. / Real basins include more stores and transfers.

Our interactive model divides a stated rainfall input into simplified pathways. Check that the parts add to the input within that model. Then identify what it leaves out: time delays, storage changes, evaporation and complex drainage routes may matter in a real basin. This is not a reason to reject the model; it tells us the question it can answer. It illustrates how changing a surface condition can change the split, but does not predict the exact discharge of a named river after a real storm.

Brief check: Does the classroom split predict every real river response?
Listen for: No. It omits important processes and timing.

On screen: Meltwater: Water produced when ice melts. Melting ice feeds a stream. / Storage: Water held in a place or form. Ice holds water before it is released. / Water balance: The difference between water inputs and outputs. Inputs minus outputs change the store.

Meltwater: Water produced when ice melts. Example: Melting ice feeds a stream. Storage: Water held in a place or form. Example: Ice holds water before it is released. Water balance: The difference between water inputs and outputs. Example: Inputs minus outputs change the store. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

Words for today

On screen: Source: Where a river begins. A spring can begin a river. / Tributary: A smaller river joining another river. A smaller channel joins the main river. / Mouth: Where a river enters the sea or another water body. Follow flow to a lake, sea or other water body.

Source: Where a river begins. Example: A spring can begin a river. Tributary: A smaller river joining another river. Example: A smaller channel joins the main river. Mouth: Where a river enters the sea or another water body. Example: Follow flow to a lake, sea or other water body. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

Words for today

On screen: Evaporation: Liquid water becoming water vapour. Energy helps liquid water become vapour. / Condensation: Water vapour becoming liquid droplets. Cooling vapour can form cloud droplets. / Precipitation: Water falling from clouds. Rain or snow returns water to land or sea.

Evaporation: Liquid water becoming water vapour. Example: Energy helps liquid water become vapour. Condensation: Water vapour becoming liquid droplets. Example: Cooling vapour can form cloud droplets. Precipitation: Water falling from clouds. Example: Rain or snow returns water to land or sea. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Ice is a water store

On screen: Snow and ice hold water over time. / Melting releases water to other stores and flows.

A glacier stores water as ice. Snowfall can add to that store, while melting can release liquid water. A store is an amount held at a time; a flow is movement into or out of it. Show a storage box with incoming and outgoing arrows. This distinction helps us understand why a large river flow does not necessarily mean the ice store is growing. Water in the river may come from rainfall as well as melting. Follow each input separately before making a claim about the stored ice.

Brief check: Is river flow the same quantity as water stored in ice?
Listen for: No. One is a flow and the other a store.

Water supply depends on timing

On screen: People need water when and where they use it. / Seasonal patterns matter as well as annual totals.

A yearly water total can conceal periods of shortage or high flow. Households, farming, hydropower and ecosystems may need water at different times. Explain why changes in snow and ice storage can alter the timing of release, not merely the total amount. A recommendation needs seasonal flow information and demand, while long-term predictions require more than one classroom calculation. Separate measured trends from a single unusual year. This connects the physical water system to human needs without pretending the simple diagram includes every management factor.

Brief check: Why is an annual total alone insufficient for supply planning?
Listen for: It can hide when water is available and when it is needed.

A river has a connected course

On screen: Source: where the river begins. / Mouth: where it enters another water body.

A river carries water along a connected course from its source towards its mouth. The source is where the named river begins, while the mouth is where it enters another water body. Downstream means following the flow; upstream is towards the source against that direction. Trace the course before naming individual parts. A map may show bends and junctions, but page position alone does not define downstream. Water generally moves from higher towards lower elevation, so we must use the network and flow information rather than assume rivers always run towards the bottom of the page.

Brief check: Does downstream always mean towards the bottom of a map?
Listen for: No. Follow the river’s actual flow direction.

Use a named river and a separate model

On screen: The Thames flows through London towards the North Sea. / A schematic explains connections, not exact bends.

The Thames has its source in the Cotswolds and flows through London towards its estuary and the North Sea. Locate the named places on an appropriate map. Then use the simple source-to-mouth schematic to explain tributaries and confluences. Keep its purpose clear: a straight arrow can show a connection without reproducing the river’s exact shape or distances. A named real river and a fictional exercise network can be used in the same lesson if pupils know which facts belong to which source.

Brief check: Does a simple source-to-mouth arrow show every real bend of the Thames?
Listen for: No. It is a schematic connection.

Water moves between stores

On screen: Water can be stored in oceans, ice, soil and groundwater. / Processes move water between stores.

The water cycle describes water moving between places and changing state. Oceans, lakes, ice, soil and groundwater are stores. A store holds water; a process moves it or changes its form. Trace one possible route rather than suggesting that every drop follows the same circle at the same speed. Water can remain in different stores for very different times. A classroom diagram simplifies a large connected system, so its arrows should help explain specific transfers rather than become a sequence memorised without meaning.

Brief check: Is soil water a store or a transfer?
Listen for: A store.

The basin model has a boundary

On screen: A simple split can show runoff and infiltration. / Real basins include more stores and transfers.

Our interactive model divides a stated rainfall input into simplified pathways. Check that the parts add to the input within that model. Then identify what it leaves out: time delays, storage changes, evaporation and complex drainage routes may matter in a real basin. This is not a reason to reject the model; it tells us the question it can answer. It illustrates how changing a surface condition can change the split, but does not predict the exact discharge of a named river after a real storm.

Brief check: Does the classroom split predict every real river response?
Listen for: No. It omits important processes and timing.

17–22 min · Worked example

Worked example · Design a counterexample · Compare short-term flow with long-term storage

On screen: Calculate the change in the ice store. / Separate storage from flowing water.

Demonstrate this complete example: More melt may increase release now while reducing the stored ice available later. A bank account analogy helps: a larger withdrawal today does not prove a larger future balance. Actual runoff also depends on precipitation and season. Explain each operation or causal link aloud. Then give pupils the different case on the next step.

Why is “more melt now means more water forever” weak?

On screen:

Use the worked example’s method on this different case. Invite pupils’ reasoning before showing: It ignores depletion of the ice store and other water inputs. A short-term flow increase does not establish a permanent supply increase.

Worked example · Design a counterexample · Use river-network vocabulary correctly

On screen: Locate source, tributary, confluence and mouth. / Follow connected channels downstream.

Demonstrate this complete example: A tributary joins the main river at a confluence. The source begins the river; the mouth is where it enters another water body. Follow the arrows downstream instead of treating every branching line as a river splitting. Explain each operation or causal link aloud. Then give pupils the different case on the next step.

Two streams join. What is the meeting point called?

On screen:

Use the worked example’s method on this different case. Invite pupils’ reasoning before showing: A confluence. A confluence is a junction; a watershed is a drainage divide.

Worked example · Design a counterexample · Compare surface and underground pathways

On screen: Label changes of state correctly. / Connect evaporation, condensation and precipitation.

Demonstrate this complete example: One drop runs over the surface into a stream; another infiltrates and may move slowly through soil and rock. Storage and pathway affect timing. Water does not follow one fixed loop at one universal speed. Explain each operation or causal link aloud. Then give pupils the different case on the next step.

After rainfall, must all water reach the river immediately?

On screen:

Use the worked example’s method on this different case. Invite pupils’ reasoning before showing: No; some infiltrates or remains in stores. Different pathways and stores produce different travel times.

Words for today

On screen: Meltwater: Water produced when ice melts. Melting ice feeds a stream. / Storage: Water held in a place or form. Ice holds water before it is released. / Water balance: The difference between water inputs and outputs. Inputs minus outputs change the store.

Words for today

On screen: Evaporation: Liquid water becoming water vapour. Energy helps liquid water become vapour. / Condensation: Water vapour becoming liquid droplets. Cooling vapour can form cloud droplets. / Precipitation: Water falling from clouds. Rain or snow returns water to land or sea.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Ice is a water store

On screen: Snow and ice hold water over time. / Melting releases water to other stores and flows.

A glacier stores water as ice. Snowfall can add to that store, while melting can release liquid water. A store is an amount held at a time; a flow is movement into or out of it. Show a storage box with incoming and outgoing arrows. This distinction helps us understand why a large river flow does not necessarily mean the ice store is growing. Water in the river may come from rainfall as well as melting. Follow each input separately before making a claim about the stored ice.

Brief check: Is river flow the same quantity as water stored in ice?
Listen for: No. One is a flow and the other a store.

Water supply depends on timing

On screen: People need water when and where they use it. / Seasonal patterns matter as well as annual totals.

A yearly water total can conceal periods of shortage or high flow. Households, farming, hydropower and ecosystems may need water at different times. Explain why changes in snow and ice storage can alter the timing of release, not merely the total amount. A recommendation needs seasonal flow information and demand, while long-term predictions require more than one classroom calculation. Separate measured trends from a single unusual year. This connects the physical water system to human needs without pretending the simple diagram includes every management factor.

Brief check: Why is an annual total alone insufficient for supply planning?
Listen for: It can hide when water is available and when it is needed.

A river has a connected course

On screen: Source: where the river begins. / Mouth: where it enters another water body.

A river carries water along a connected course from its source towards its mouth. The source is where the named river begins, while the mouth is where it enters another water body. Downstream means following the flow; upstream is towards the source against that direction. Trace the course before naming individual parts. A map may show bends and junctions, but page position alone does not define downstream. Water generally moves from higher towards lower elevation, so we must use the network and flow information rather than assume rivers always run towards the bottom of the page.

Brief check: Does downstream always mean towards the bottom of a map?
Listen for: No. Follow the river’s actual flow direction.

Use a named river and a separate model

On screen: The Thames flows through London towards the North Sea. / A schematic explains connections, not exact bends.

The Thames has its source in the Cotswolds and flows through London towards its estuary and the North Sea. Locate the named places on an appropriate map. Then use the simple source-to-mouth schematic to explain tributaries and confluences. Keep its purpose clear: a straight arrow can show a connection without reproducing the river’s exact shape or distances. A named real river and a fictional exercise network can be used in the same lesson if pupils know which facts belong to which source.

Brief check: Does a simple source-to-mouth arrow show every real bend of the Thames?
Listen for: No. It is a schematic connection.

Water moves between stores

On screen: Water can be stored in oceans, ice, soil and groundwater. / Processes move water between stores.

The water cycle describes water moving between places and changing state. Oceans, lakes, ice, soil and groundwater are stores. A store holds water; a process moves it or changes its form. Trace one possible route rather than suggesting that every drop follows the same circle at the same speed. Water can remain in different stores for very different times. A classroom diagram simplifies a large connected system, so its arrows should help explain specific transfers rather than become a sequence memorised without meaning.

Brief check: Is soil water a store or a transfer?
Listen for: A store.

The basin model has a boundary

On screen: A simple split can show runoff and infiltration. / Real basins include more stores and transfers.

Our interactive model divides a stated rainfall input into simplified pathways. Check that the parts add to the input within that model. Then identify what it leaves out: time delays, storage changes, evaporation and complex drainage routes may matter in a real basin. This is not a reason to reject the model; it tells us the question it can answer. It illustrates how changing a surface condition can change the split, but does not predict the exact discharge of a named river after a real storm.

Brief check: Does the classroom split predict every real river response?
Listen for: No. It omits important processes and timing.

7B · Week 29 · Lesson 1 · sections 5.3

40-minute route: recall 4, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 8, worked example 5, practice 10, check 5, exit 3. Divide each section between the topics in combined lessons. Timings are estimates.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

Does river width alone tell us its discharge?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. No. Discharge also depends on cross-sectional area and flow velocity. Connect this to today’s task: Build a drainage basin.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can draw a drainage divide from high ground.

On screen: Today’s task: Build a drainage basin / You will make a basin diagram or measurement comparison. / Trace drainage towards the river. / Show watersheds between basins. / Distinguish width, depth, velocity and discharge.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: a basin diagram or measurement comparison. Explain the three criteria: Trace drainage towards the river. Show watersheds between basins. Distinguish width, depth, velocity and discharge. The independent task uses this case: Model: two tributaries join one main channel inside a ridge boundary.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Drainage basin: Land draining into one river system. Trace land drained by one river network. / Watershed: The boundary between drainage basins. A ridge can separate two basins. / Discharge: The volume of water passing a point per second. Volume per second needs area and velocity.

Drainage basin: Land draining into one river system. Example: Trace land drained by one river network. Watershed: The boundary between drainage basins. Example: A ridge can separate two basins. Discharge: The volume of water passing a point per second. Example: Volume per second needs area and velocity. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Compare upper, middle and lower course

On screen: Channel form and valley shape change along the river. / Tributaries and local conditions affect the pattern.

The upper course is nearer the source, while the lower course is nearer the mouth; the middle course lies between. In many school examples, the upper valley is narrower and the channel smaller, while tributaries add water downstream and the lower channel becomes wider and deeper. The valley floor may also broaden. Treat these as patterns to investigate rather than absolute rules at every point. Rock, local slope, water inputs and human alterations can produce variation. Describe the actual source evidence before applying a general model. Course position provides a geographical framework for comparing channel measurements; width, depth and discharge then help explain what differs and why.

Brief check: Should a general downstream pattern replace checking the actual measurements?
Listen for: No. Use the model alongside the source evidence.

A channel has width, depth and velocity

On screen: Width and depth describe channel size. / Velocity describes water speed.

A river’s width and depth describe the channel cross-section, while velocity is the speed of flowing water. These are different quantities. A wide river is not necessarily carrying more water each second than a narrower but deeper and faster one. Point to the width across the surface and depth down into the section, then follow the flow arrow to show velocity. Measurements need units and representative methods because depth and speed can vary across a real channel. Our simple rectangular model makes the relationship easier to calculate.

Brief check: Does width alone establish how much water passes each second?
Listen for: No. Depth and velocity also matter.

Discharge is volume per time

On screen: Discharge measures water passing a section. / This model uses area × mean velocity.

Discharge is the volume of water passing a cross-section per unit of time. In a simplified rectangular section, width times depth gives area. Multiply that area by mean velocity to estimate discharge. Metres times metres gives square metres, and multiplying by metres per second gives cubic metres per second. Explain the units using a block of water moving past the section. Real channels require suitable measurements of shape and velocity, so the model’s neat numbers are a teaching example rather than a complete field method.

Brief check: What does discharge measure?
Listen for: Volume of water passing per unit of time.

Compare all the relevant quantities

On screen: A larger area can carry more water. / Faster flow can also increase discharge.

Compare two model rivers by calculating each discharge, not by choosing the one that looks widest. A section of ten square metres at two metres per second carries twenty cubic metres per second in the model. A section of twenty square metres at half a metre per second carries ten. The example shows why a visible dimension alone is insufficient. Keep the area and velocity labels beside the calculation. If the source omits necessary values, “we need more information” is a valid conclusion rather than an invitation to guess.

Brief check: Can we choose the greater discharge without depth or velocity information?
Listen for: Not reliably from width alone.

River changes vary along the course

On screen: Inputs and channel conditions change downstream. / Use evidence instead of absolute rules.

Tributaries can add water downstream, while channel size and flow conditions can change. These patterns help explain river variation, but they are not a guarantee that every measurement increases at every point and moment. Rainfall, withdrawals, storage and channel form can affect observations. State whether the source describes a particular section, time or general pattern. A measurement taken during one event should not automatically become a permanent characteristic of the whole river. This keeps the calculation connected to the geographical context in which it was made.

Brief check: Does one high-flow measurement describe the river at all times?
Listen for: No. Time and conditions affect flow.

The divide is not the river itself. Explain each operation or causal link aloud. Then give pupils the different case on the next step.

The divide is not the river itself. Explain why one choice fits and why the other does not. The ridge can separate downhill flow paths. Then invite a volunteer for one turn if useful. Sediment journey

7B · Week 29 · Lesson 2 · sections 5.4

40-minute route: recall 4, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 8, worked example 5, practice 10, check 5, exit 3. Divide each section between the topics in combined lessons. Timings are estimates.

0–4 min · Starter and recall

Is moving sediment the same as depositing it?

On screen:

Invite an explanation before revealing. No. Transport moves material; deposition leaves it behind when conditions change. Connect this to today’s task: Sediment journey.

4–6 min · Today’s learning goal

I can distinguish removing, moving and dropping sediment.

On screen: Today’s task: Sediment journey / You will make a sediment storyboard. / Use remove, carry and lay down for the three actions. / Link the actions in a sediment journey. / Explain how flow and particle properties affect settling.

Show the goal and preview the actual product: a sediment storyboard. Explain the three criteria: Use remove, carry and lay down for the three actions. Link the actions in a sediment journey. Explain how flow and particle properties affect settling. The independent task uses this case: A pebble is loosened, moves downstream and settles where flow slows.

6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Erosion: Wearing away and removing material. Water removes material from a bank. / Transportation: Moving sediment. A pebble is carried downstream. / Deposition: Dropping sediment. A pebble settles as flow conditions change.

Erosion: Wearing away and removing material. Example: Water removes material from a bank. Transportation: Moving sediment. Example: A pebble is carried downstream. Deposition: Dropping sediment. Example: A pebble settles as flow conditions change. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Rivers erode, transport and deposit

On screen: Erosion removes material. / Transport moves it; deposition leaves it behind.

A river can remove material, carry it and deposit it farther along its course. These are distinct processes that can occur in different parts of the same system. Trace one particle from a bank into moving water and then to a deposit. The river does not need to be either eroding or depositing everywhere at once. Local flow and available material influence what happens. Naming the process accurately helps us explain a landform rather than treating every visible change as erosion.

Brief check: Is moving material the same process as leaving it behind?
Listen for: No. Transport and deposition are different.

Erosion has different mechanisms

On screen: Water can remove weakened material. / Carried particles can abrade the bed and banks.

Flowing water can act on the channel directly and use carried sediment to wear surfaces. Hydraulic action describes the force of water on the channel, while abrasion involves carried material scraping or striking the bed and banks. Solution removes some soluble material chemically, and attrition wears transported particles as they collide. Introduce the actions through the diagram before adding the terms. These processes can work together, and their importance depends on flow, rock and sediment conditions. A list of names should not replace the explanation of what each action does.

Brief check: Which process uses carried particles to wear the channel?
Listen for: Abrasion.

Particles move in different ways

On screen: Large particles can roll; smaller ones can bounce. / Fine material can be suspended; dissolved material travels in solution.

Traction describes particles rolling or sliding along the bed. Saltation involves bouncing movement. Fine particles can be held in suspension, while dissolved material travels in solution. Show each position relative to the bed and water column. The transport mode depends on particle properties and flow conditions, so size alone is not a universal rule. A clear model can compare particles under stated similar conditions. If density changes as well as size, we cannot claim that size alone explains all the differences in movement.

Brief check: Is dissolved material simply a visible particle floating at the surface?
Listen for: No. It travels in solution.

Deposition depends on carrying capacity

On screen: Slower or changed flow can release sediment. / Different materials settle under different conditions.

When flow conditions no longer keep material moving, sediment may be deposited. Coarser particles often settle before finer ones under a simple comparable setup, but density, shape and flow also matter. Explain what stays constant in the demonstration before making a prediction. A pile of sediment can show deposition without telling us the complete history of its transport. 6–9 min · Key vocabulary

Words for today

On screen: Erosion: Wearing away and removing material. Water removes material from a bank. / Transportation: Moving sediment. A pebble is carried downstream. / Deposition: Dropping sediment. A pebble settles as flow conditions change.

Erosion: Wearing away and removing material. Example: Water removes material from a bank. Transportation: Moving sediment. Example: A pebble is carried downstream. Deposition: Dropping sediment. Example: A pebble settles as flow conditions change. Point to the relevant part of each picture. A named example supports the meaning; exact quantities belong to the supplied case. Invite one use of a word in the task context.

9–17 min · Teacher explanation

Rivers erode, transport and deposit

On screen: Erosion removes material. / Transport moves it; deposition leaves it behind.

A river can remove material, carry it and deposit it farther along its course. These are distinct processes that can occur in different parts of the same system. Trace one particle from a bank into moving water and then to a deposit. The river does not need to be either eroding or depositing everywhere at once. Local flow and available material influence what happens. Naming the process accurately helps us explain a landform rather than treating every visible change as erosion.

Brief check: Is moving material the same process as leaving it behind?
Listen for: No. Transport and deposition are different.

Erosion has different mechanisms

On screen: Water can remove weakened material. / Carried particles can abrade the bed and banks.

Flowing water can act on the channel directly and use carried sediment to wear surfaces. Hydraulic action describes the force of water on the channel, while abrasion involves carried material scraping or striking the bed and banks. Solution removes some soluble material chemically, and attrition wears transported particles as they collide. Introduce the actions through the diagram before adding the terms. These processes can work together, and their importance depends on flow, rock and sediment conditions. A list of names should not replace the explanation of what each action does.

Brief check: Which process uses carried particles to wear the channel?
Listen for: Abrasion.

Particles move in different ways

On screen: Large particles can roll; smaller ones can bounce. / Fine material can be suspended; dissolved material travels in solution.

Traction describes particles rolling or sliding along the bed. Saltation involves bouncing movement. Fine particles can be held in suspension, while dissolved material travels in solution. Show each position relative to the bed and water column. The transport mode depends on particle properties and flow conditions, so size alone is not a universal rule. A clear model can compare particles under stated similar conditions. If density changes as well as size, we cannot claim that size alone explains all the differences in movement.

Brief check: Is dissolved material simply a visible particle floating at the surface?
Listen for: No. It travels in solution.

Deposition depends on carrying capacity

On screen: Slower or changed flow can release sediment. / Different materials settle under different conditions.

When flow conditions no longer keep material moving, sediment may be deposited. Coarser particles often settle before finer ones under a simple comparable setup, but density, shape and flow also matter. Explain what stays constant in the demonstration before making a prediction. A pile of sediment can show deposition without telling us the complete history of its transport. Use the source conditions to interpret the sequence and avoid saying every particle follows an identical rule in every river. The mechanism is a change in the ability to carry material.

Brief check: Why should density be considered in a settling comparison?
Listen for: It can affect settling as well as particle size.

On screen:
